While CBI is working on an answer, its button gives off a soft pulse.
The tech's day on the Dispatch map now shows their clocked hours, about how long they drive between jobs, and a Tomorrow view, with Call, Text and Locate buttons.
When CBI offers to do something for you, the phone app shows its questions with a Go button too. On the web and the phone, the Service address suggests real addresses as you type.
Ask CrewBarn on the phone (More menu) takes a photo too.

Ask CBI how to do something, like "how do I create a job?", and it offers a walkthrough: tap Walk me through it and CBI opens the page and walks you through it step by step. CBI steps aside while you follow along; tap the CBI button to come back to the same chat.

CBI can also do it for you. For a new job, a quote or a task it shows the few questions it needs: fill them in and press Go. If anything is missing, CBI asks, and when it asks what time or which tech, it tells you who is free then.
Booking a job through CBI with a tech who already has something at that time? The Confirm says so, and who is free instead.

On the Dispatch map, click a tech (or their name in the list) to see their day: what they're on right now and for how long, each job with when they got there and how long they were on it, their to-dos, and a one-line summary.
Task circles now respond as soon as you mark a to-do done or reopen it. If saving fails, the circle returns to its previous state and shows an error.

CBI stays open while you work: the page beside it is no longer dimmed, so you can click a job or customer CBI shows you and look around while the chat stays put. On a wide screen the page moves over to make room. CBI also knows which job or customer you have open, so you can ask about "this customer".
Show CBI a photo: tap the camera in CBI (or paste a picture on the web) and ask "what part is this?" or "do we have this in stock?". It works when CBI runs on Claude, and photos aren't saved.
"Quote Rita good, better, best": CBI drafts the estimate with two to four options at your price-list prices, with a trip charge in every option if you ask. It stays a draft for you to check and send.
"Tell Rita I'm 15 minutes out": the running-late text now gives the time you'll get there, and the late watch holds you to that time.
CBI starts reading its answer aloud after the first sentence instead of waiting for the whole reply.

Close out a job by voice: "done at Rita's, swapped the unit, used the new part and an hour of labor, mark it complete". CBI saves the note, adds the items at your price-list prices, and sets the status, all on one Confirm. If the job still needs a signature or photos, CBI tells you what's missing and saves the note and parts anyway.

"Invoice Rita and text her the link": CBI makes the invoice from the job, and after you Confirm it texts the customer a link to view and pay it in your customer portal. The customer needs portal access or an email on file to open it; if they have neither, CBI leaves the invoice as a draft and tells you. Ask again and it resends the link. Stocked parts that need a QR scan are still added in the app.

CBI can do more of the day: ask "what's the gate code at Rita's?", "who's free Thursday afternoon?", "tell Rita I'm 10 minutes out", "move the Smith job to Friday at 2 and give it to Ian", or "what's my day?" for your stops in order with gate codes and parts to bring.
Texting a customer and moving a job always wait for your Confirm, and texts only go to customers who agreed to them.

Call summaries know who's who: whoever answers with your company's name is your staff, not the customer, and each summary starts with the customer's name (or Caller), what they wanted, and what's next. CBI's day summary reads like a short dispatcher's briefing.
CBI is much faster. It now runs on a fast model of its own (Claude Haiku 5.5, change it under Settings → CBI AI), and it no longer re-reads all its instructions on every step.
Every call and voicemail now gets a one-line summary when its transcript arrives, so "Hey CrewBarn, summarize today's calls" answers in seconds: how many calls, and the ones that need someone.
The model list adds Claude Haiku 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5.

CBI in the phone app now reads the conversation you have open in Messages. Ask it to set up a job from a text or call and the caller's phone number goes on the customer, and the conversation shows on the new job.
Customers can now press 9 on any CBI call to stop them: they're tagged Do not call and CBI never calls them again. Every customer call ends by telling them so.
CBI only dials US and Canadian numbers, and stops for the day at your daily limit (100 calls to start, change it in Shop Rules → Late techs). When it does, the office gets a notice in the bell.

Quiet hours now hold every automated email to staff, not just task reminders: job status and reminder emails to a tech or the office, the stale-jobs digest, open-visit alerts, and access requests all arrive when quiet hours end.

CBI's running-late calls are smarter. A late that flickers on and off as a tech's GPS wobbles no longer calls anyone twice: CBI calls the tech and the customer at most once a day per job. If the tech already called or texted the customer about it, CBI calls nobody and the office isn't flashed.

When a voicemail picks up, CBI waits for the beep and leaves a short message with your office number, instead of the press-1 menu, and it no longer counts as reaching the customer. If the tech doesn't answer CBI's call, the office sees the late straight away instead of after the tech's head start.

New Employee settings under Connect → Team. Quiet hours (8 PM to 7 AM to start): nobody gets task reminder emails, phones don't buzz, and CBI doesn't call a tech or a customer. Reminders arrive when quiet hours end, and a tech running late for a job still gets the alert.
Task reminder emails can be switched off for everyone there, and each person can keep their own quiet hours and task emails on their staff record.

Daily duties now start from a date, set to yesterday, so old invoices and estimates no longer fill everyone's to-dos. To-dos already made for older records close on the next hourly check. Change the date, or look back through everything, on the same page.

Daily duty to-dos no longer send "Task due soon" and "Task overdue" emails. Someone who owned a busy duty, like answering calls and texts, could get hundreds. The to-dos are still on the Responsibilities board and in My to-dos, and your other tasks still email reminders as before.

A job's CBI calls now show how the call is going as it happens: ringing, answered and on the call, then how long it lasted. Before, a call said Calling until it was over. A call CBI connected no longer offers Create job from this call, since it's already about the job.

The running-late calls are now CBI calls. Find their scripts under Connect → CBI AI → Calls → CBI calls, switch them all off in one place under CBI AI → Allowed actions, and see every call CBI made, and to whom, in CBI's Activity. The job's Messages and History tabs and the Schedule's CBI: call customer button say CBI too.

Pick the voice for each automated call script: thirteen natural AI voices, women's and men's, each described (warm, calm, deep, upbeat...), plus how it sounds: friendly, calm, professional or upbeat. Press Listen in the editor to hear it before you save. The whole call, from the message to Connecting you and Goodbye, now speaks in that one voice.

Customers who get the running-late call can now press 2 to talk to their technician (press 1 is still your office). Every call script has a When they press 2 choice, and Test call can really put you through to the office or to a phone standing in for the tech.

A customer's invoice email subject is now built from a dropdown: pick Insert a tag for their work order or PO number, the invoice number or total, the customer name or account number, the service location, or a customer or job field you added. It shows an example of the finished subject as you go.

Automated calls now have scripts you can edit, like your text and email templates, with the same tags (customer name, start time, how late, ETA). Find them under Connect → Phone, text & email → Automated call scripts, with a Test call button to hear one on your phone.
Press 1: a tech who gets the running-late call can press 1 to be connected straight to the customer, on a recorded call kept on the job. A customer who gets a call can press 1 to talk to your office.

Calling the customer when their tech is late: off by default. Choose Only when the office presses Call customer, or Automatically, under Shop Rules → GPS check-in. Each customer (Contacts tab) and each job can follow that or say Never; customers tagged do-not-call are never called.
Every automated call is kept on its job: who was called, whether they answered and for how long, and what they pressed. See it in the job's Messages and History tabs.

A tech who may be late now hears it first: a red flashing Running late pop-up in the phone app with the customer, how far away they are, and a Call customer button, plus an automated phone call telling them to open the app and call.

Dispatch is told a few minutes later (5 by default, set it under Shop Rules → GPS check-in). If the tech calls the customer first, the Schedule button doesn't flash for it, and the Schedule page shows who called and when.
Daily duties from Responsibilities stay off the calendar, in the office and in the phone app. They’re on each person’s to-do list and the Today board.

New: Responsibilities, under Tool Shed → Team. Give jobs, estimates, billing, the books, parts and people each an owner and a backup. Every hour CrewBarn puts what needs doing on that person's to-do list, one item at a time, and takes it off once it's done.

A job that didn't get finished lands on the office's list and the tech's. Finished jobs nobody invoiced, invoices nobody sent, money still in a truck, bills coming due and time off waiting for an answer each land on the right person's list.
The Today board shows who has what, what's overdue and what got done. Tap a person to see their list. Each area's checks can be turned off, and you set how long before each one counts.

When a tech may be late for a job, the Schedule button flashes red and blue, like a police light, until somebody in the office presses Got it on the Schedule page. If nobody does within 5 minutes, a toast pops up on every office screen. Turn it off, or change the minutes, under Shop Rules → GPS check-in.

Calls a tech makes from a job in the phone app are tied to that job. Once the call is transcribed, CrewBarn writes a note on the job, records when the tech said they'd arrive, and if the customer asked for another day, puts a move request in front of the office. The schedule never moves without the office.
Correcting an expense or a vendor bill now corrects your books too. Fix a $500 typo to $50 and the reports say $50. Expenses and bills edited before today are corrected the next time they're saved.
Moving an approved reimbursement back to pending or rejected takes it off what you owe the employee.
A payment taken on a draft invoice is held as a customer deposit until the invoice is issued, instead of making receivables go negative.
Saving a vendor bill without picking its category no longer resets the category.

Take your secure files with you: Company Files can export every company and customer secure file as one encrypted zip that opens in 7-Zip (or Keka on a Mac). The password is shown to you once and CrewBarn doesn't keep it. API keys can no longer reach secure files at all.

Deleting or voiding an expense, a vendor bill or an invoice now takes it off your books too, so reports stop counting what isn't there. A bill with payments, or a reimbursed expense, asks you to reverse those first.

A customer paying a Stripe charge you had voided no longer brings it back as paid. You get an alert to refund it instead. GoDaddy sales are recorded once even if the phone and the office both record them.
Marking a draft invoice paid issues it first, so it's dated and on your books. Drafts never count as overdue.
Saving one field on a payroll profile no longer resets the rest of it to zero.
Techs who see only their own jobs now see only their own estimates (also on the calendar), their own GPS device, and messages about their jobs. They can't approve their own NTE increase.

Estimates can offer good, better and best. Press + New tier under the line items: what you have becomes Good and Better starts as a copy, so you only change what's different. Add Best the same way, rename any of them, say what sets each apart, and mark one Recommended.
Your customer sees each option with its price in their portal and picks one. The job and invoice carry only the option they chose. Mark Approved asks which one they took when they say yes in person.
Customer app settings (Tool Shed → Customer app) save themselves a moment after each change. There's no Save button to forget, and the build buttons wait until it says All changes saved.
The customer portal's intro film and tour keep the customer's phone screen on while they play, instead of the phone dimming and locking partway through.

Switching storage now moves your files: to your own bucket, back to CrewBarn storage, or from one bucket to another. The copy starts right away, and everything stays visible meanwhile, including catalogs, which used to show as missing until the copy finished. Storage & maps shows how the move is going.

Before a text goes to a customer who hasn't agreed to texts, CrewBarn asks whether they agreed. Say yes and it's sent, and their agreement is saved on their record with your name and the date. Replying to someone who texted you first goes straight through.
Calls recorded through CrewBarn now tell the customer "This call may be recorded", and click-to-call only rings a staff or company phone first.
A new franchise owner gets a link to set their own password instead of a password in the email. Emailing an invoice to an address that isn't on the customer now needs permission to edit invoices.

A customer's own work-order form is now filled in when the job is completed: the date, times in and out, technician, work performed, parts, their WO and PO numbers, and the signature go into its blanks. A completion page still follows as proof of the work.

On the job's Doc tab, each blank shows what goes in it, and you can change it. Preview on the form shows where everything will land before the job is done, with anything still missing named in grey. A finished job can be filled again after a late signature or a correction.
The completion page now shows each line's unit price (it printed $0.00), the technician's name rather than their email, and times in the job's own time zone.

The API guide (Tool Shed → Developers → API guide) now covers the rest of what an API key can call: jobs, estimates, invoices, customers, payments, catalog, inventory, equipment, subcontractors and messaging.

API keys can no longer change the bank details customers pay into, read the Google Maps key, save the legal reviewer's key, or change Google review settings and replies. Deleting a subcontractor now asks for your password and a reason like every other delete.

Google reviews can answer themselves (Tool Shed → Google reviews → Answer reviews automatically). Choose what each star rating gets: 4–5 stars can post a reply on their own after a wait you set, and 1–3 stars only ever get a draft for you to read and post.
Replies are written by your AI from what the customer said, if you allow it, or from your own reply list, which fills in their first name, your company name and your phone number.
Any review without a reply, old ones included, has a Write a draft button. A draft that's waiting to post shows when it will go up. You can edit and post it yourself, or stop it posting on its own.

"Fill in map coordinates" now says how many of the addresses it couldn't place still have an open job. Those jobs are missing from the dispatch map. It handles them first, and each example names the customer with a link, so you can add the address.
A Google Maps key is checked before it's saved, in setup and in Tool Shed → Storage & maps. A wrong paste no longer replaces a working key, and setup keeps your saved key if you leave the box blank.
The Maps "Test key" button no longer hangs on "Testing…". It says whether Google refused the key (wrong key, or not allowed on this site) or didn't answer.
"Fill in map coordinates" says why it skipped an address (no address on file, Google found nothing, Google refused, or the position couldn't be saved) and lists the first few.
Finishing a job at check-out now sets off your "job completed" automations (review requests and the like). It used to skip them, because the job was marked complete before its status moved.

If a job's status can't move at check-in or check-out (a rule, or a status that needs an invoice first), the tech now sees why and the office gets a note on the job. The job is still marked complete. Before, nothing was said.
Status texts go only to customers who have agreed to texts, on the customer or their main contact, like every other automatic text. Emails, and texts to your techs and office, are unchanged.
Status messages and automations now also go out when a sub's update moves your job, and a sub's late update no longer reopens a job you closed or cancelled.
Webhooks need a public https:// address. Older ones saved with http:// stop sending until you update them.

Order low stock automatically (Settings → Inventory): when a stocked item drops to its reorder threshold, CrewBarn adds it to a draft purchase order for its vendor. Nothing is sent: you check the draft and mark it ordered, and stock already on order counts, so nothing is ordered twice.
Restock vans to par (Settings → Inventory): when a van carries fewer of an item than its par, the shop gets a transfer request for the difference, for the van's tech to confirm when it arrives.
Needs ordered shows what's already on order for each item, and takes it off the suggested quantity.

New completion requirements for clients who send their own work orders: their WO # entered on the job, and their work order attached. Set them in Preferences, on a job type, or on a customer account (a chain's parent account covers every store).

Mark a job's photo or file as Client WO: in the job's photos and documents on the web, or with the photo label on the phone. A photo of the signed paper sheet counts. When a job is missing it, the phone's close-out opens the camera ready to label it, and asks for their WO # if that's missing too.

Their WO # and PO # now print on every invoice: in Job details on your current layout, or under the job after Templates → Restore CrewBarn defaults on your invoice. They also show on statements and in the customer portal, and a customer's invoice email subject can include them with {{job.their_work_order_number}} and {{job.their_po_number}}.

Photos and files work again for companies on their own Cloudflare storage. Without a public web address saved for the bucket, every image was broken; CrewBarn now serves them itself. Switching to your own bucket also copies your existing files into it, and every saved link moves with them.

Status flow rules: when two rules cover the same move, the one from the exact starting status now wins over an Any status rule. A rule's own requirements (schedule, technician, signature, photos) always apply. Each rule shows who may make the move, and you can change it.

Jobs you sub out: the signature the sub's tech takes now counts as a signature on your job, and their Before and After photos keep their labels. If your Complete was waiting on that proof, the job moves on when it arrives.

Completion rules: set the proof every job needs in Preferences (a signature, a number of photos, a Before and an After photo, parts and labour). A job type or a customer account can set its own rule: require more, or turn one off for that customer. A chain's parent account sets it for every store. A job can't be marked Complete, or moved to any status after it, until its proof is in, on the web, the phone or CBI.

When the proof really can't be had (the store is closed at night, nobody to sign), someone with "Complete without proof" in Roles can complete the job anyway with a reason. Owner, Admin and Dispatcher have it to start. The reason, who gave it and what was missing show on the job.

A status can now require the job to be Complete, or to have an invoice, before it can be used. Moving a completed job back to work reopens it, so it's checked again next time. "An invoice needs the job Complete" is a setting in Preferences. Turn it off if you bill progress or deposits.
Techs can label photos Before or After, also after they're taken. Money taken on a job before it has an invoice is now recorded as a down payment, and it's applied when the invoice is made.

Portal invites are now secured by a 6-digit code sent to the email you invited. Your customer can accept with a new account, an existing one, or Google, even under a different email: the code to the invited address proves it's them. The contact shows which email they sign in with.

Taking someone off a customer account now ends their portal access to that account only. Delete or deactivate the contact, or use Remove portal access on it. They keep their portal and their other accounts: a property manager taken off one property's account still sees the others. Their access to that account's jobs, invoices and assets ends at once, and signing in again doesn't bring it back; only a new invite does.

Someone on several of your customer accounts (a property manager, say) now sees each account in the portal by the name it's listed under, and moves between them by name. Links in your emails and texts open on the account the job or invoice belongs to.

CBI now answers "who are our techs" from your Staff & crews list: everyone marked Works as a technician (an owner who works jobs counts), with office staff listed separately. People removed from Staff & crews no longer show up, in that answer or in crew lists.

Sub companies on the free plan: the phone app no longer offers what the free plan leaves out (new jobs, estimates, assets, receipts, payments), and explains once when a screen needs a paid plan. Their techs now get the drive-time ETA on a job, the company's tracking hours, and the job's work order form.
When a sub's tech closes out a job as complete, the company that sent it now gets "finished the job" on its copy.

Customer tags now come from your Tags library (Tool Shed → Tags). The customer form offers your active tags in their colors, and you can add your own. Rename a tag and every customer that has it follows; remove one and it comes off them.
Every company starts with the seven tags the form used to have built in (vip, commercial, recurring, warning, do-not-call, referred, priority), so tags already on customers stay put.

Every sub now gets your jobs in its own CrewBarn. A sub that isn't on CrewBarn yet has to accept an invite before you can send it work: Sub this out says so and lets you invite them on the spot. A company already on CrewBarn can take the job right away.
Staff & crews lists your earlier subs under Not on CrewBarn yet, each with Invite. Tool Shed → Subcontractors shows where each sub stands.
The old ways of reaching a sub are gone: the one-job link, the sub pages in the customer portal, sub.crewbarn.com, and connecting a sub's own software.
Customer portal sign-in now rejects signup verification attempts for accounts that are already verified. Existing customers must use the normal sign-in flow.

A provider-locked company contact stays unchanged when its linked portal user updates their profile. A person who manages one company and handles accounting for another can reach the right screens without gaining asset-control rights for the accounting company.

Connect now opens Company files and Label printer in the work app where those tools belong. View-only staff can open Modules without receiving edit rights. Asset security keys no longer appear in the scan page address.

Sending work to a company that already uses CrewBarn: under Staff & crews, add a sub company by its owner's email and CrewBarn recognizes it. No invite code. Send the first job straight away; when they accept it, you're connected and they share the documents you asked for.
You can now ask a sub for an insurance certificate that names your company as certificate holder. They upload one just for you, and only you can see it.
Missing documents no longer stop an urgent job. Sub this out tells you what's missing and offers Send anyway; the job gets a note saying what was still missing.

New switch under Tool Shed → Marketplace: Show the marketplace to my customers. Turn it off and your customers see no marketplace in their portal, so no browsing other companies and no asking them for quotes. They can still request work and quotes from you. A customer who also works with another company on CrewBarn loses it too.
Every authenticated CrewBarn page and settings area now has a guided walkthrough and workflow roadmap available from Help. Tours do not start on their own after onboarding.

Guides now cover the full job lifecycle, estimates, service agreements, customer records, schedule and dispatch, communications, accounting, inventory, assets, inspections, purchasing, documents, catalog and order book, staff and permissions, automations, Connect, AI, payments, maps, security and integrations.
AI, communication, storage and map walkthroughs include direct links to the provider setup pages when a key or outside account is required.

The first-login CrewBarn introduction now gives a fuller tour of the platform, including catalog import, estimates, service agreements, the full job lifecycle, documents, inspections, inventory, accounting, permissions, Connect settings and status-trigger automations.

Customer arrival updates are explained correctly: CrewBarn calculates an ETA from the technician’s location and sends the customer the job status and ETA. The technician’s live location stays private inside CrewBarn and is not shared with the customer.
Adding someone under Staff & crews works again. Since September 25 it stopped with an error before the person was saved; anyone you tried to add then needs adding again.

When you ask CBI to change a job's status, book a job or remember a rule, it now shows exactly what it will do with Confirm and Cancel buttons, and nothing changes until you press Confirm. Saying yes in the chat does not count, so nothing CBI reads in a job note or a customer's message can make a change on its own.
CBI also treats text in jobs, messages, call transcripts and imported records as information, never as instructions.
The dashboard has a New vs returning customers card: new customers, jobs from new customers and jobs from returning customers, by day, week, month or year, each with the period before for comparison.

A customer counts as new when their first job ever falls in that period, history brought in from another system included, so long-standing customers are never counted as new because they were imported recently.

Tax on new jobs, estimates and invoices is worked out once on the total for each tax rate, the way a register does, instead of line by line and then added up, which could land a cent off. Each line still shows its share, and the shares add up to the total.
Jobs, estimates and invoices made before today keep the tax they were made with, so nothing already sent or paid changes by a cent.

Every job has an Automations switch in its header. Off, nothing automatic goes out for that job: no status texts or emails, reminders, automation rules or dormant nudges to the tech. Jobs brought in from another system start with it off, so working through them messages nobody. Owners and admins can turn it on or off; the roles page lets you give that to others (Jobs → Edit + automations switch).

Disabling someone on Staff & crews now signs them out everywhere at once: the web, the phone app and any API keys, and their phone stops getting notifications. Before, a phone already signed in kept working until its session ran out. Their jobs, notes and time stay on file.

A job given a Canceled-type status no longer shows under Past scheduled on the dashboard or in CBI's daily stale-jobs summary, the same as on the Jobs list. Every open job still shows there and on the dormant list, however old.
Call transcription has a Test saved key button. It checks that the key for the service you chose is accepted, without transcribing anything, and tells you plainly if it was pasted wrong or revoked.

Call transcription can now use AssemblyAI, on your own AssemblyAI account: Tool Shed → Communication → Call transcription. It is the recommended choice. On real service calls it kept the office and the caller apart more cleanly and wrote part numbers and prices as digits.

OpenAI stays available. Your OpenAI key is still what CBI voice commands use, whichever you choose for calls. AssemblyAI deletes each recording and transcript on its side as soon as CrewBarn has read them.

Call transcription uses OpenAI only. Deepgram is no longer offered: a business that had chosen it now transcribes through OpenAI, with the OpenAI key under Tool Shed → Communication → Call transcription.
The green part-number chips beside spelled-out numbers are gone. Transcripts show what was transcribed, with nothing added. Calls transcribed before this keep their words as they were.

Card numbers read out on recorded calls are no longer kept. The card number, expiry date and security code are taken out of the transcript before it is saved, and before CBI uses it to draft a job. Card numbers texted in are taken out the same way.

Calls and texts saved before this are being cleaned the same way. The call recordings themselves are not changed, so take card payments with a payment link or the card reader rather than over a recorded line.
CBI can list your estimates again, and its "how long ago" counts for stale jobs are no longer negative.
A catalog now downloads once per device. After that it opens straight from the device, with no waiting on a 60 MB download each time.

Up to about 600 MB of catalogs are kept per browser, and the ones opened longest ago make room first. In the customer portal, a catalog you stop sharing is cleared from the customer's device the next time they look at your catalogs.
Tapping a part number in a catalog now brings the price printed on its row. On an estimate that is the sell price for anything you don't carry; parts you carry keep your own price.
Set your discount from a vendor once (list less 50%, for example) in the order panel, and catalog prices become your cost on purchase orders. Draft orders re-cost straight away.

Build several codes into one line: press Start a build, name it, then tap the set, its finish and its style on the page and add choices like the handing or backset. It goes on the order and the estimate as one line, priced as its pieces, with the pieces listed under it.
When the catalog prints how to order (Function + Product Code + Finish, for example), that shows beside the build as a checklist.
Customers can build their own in the portal the same way, and see the catalog prices of what they picked. When you make the estimate, a build comes in as one line at the catalog price.
Finish and style codes in brackets, like (US4) or (AS), can now be tapped, and each part gets just its own words from the table instead of the whole row.
Share a catalog with your customers: each PDF on a reference card now has a Share with customers switch. It starts off, and only the catalogs you switch on are shared.

Your customers see a Catalogs tab on your page in the customer portal. They can page through the book with its sections and Find, tap part numbers to add them to an order, add lines in their own words, and send it to you.

Orders from customers appear at the top of the Estimates page, and the bell tells you when one comes in. Create estimate makes a draft for that customer in one click: parts you carry come in at your price, anything else comes in with the customer's words and the catalog page, ready for you to price. Or decline it with a reason the customer sees.
Customers see each order they sent as Sent, Estimate ready or Declined.
Four-digit product codes in a catalog, like 7108 or 3311, can now be clicked onto an order. Any three- or four-digit number under a Product Code, Part # or SKU column heading counts too.
Prices, years, page ranges like 10-23 and phone numbers are left alone.
A catalog that prints its section names on the edge of every page now gets those as its tabs: one per section, in the book's own words, from the first page of the section to the index at the back.
A contents page set in two columns is read column by column, and lines like "Pages 28–37" on a what's-new page are no longer taken for a contents page.
Tabs are now read from the whole of a book up to 400 pages, so sections near the back of a long price book are found too.
A big PDF now shows how far its download has got while it opens: a bar, the percentage, and "Downloading 23.4 of 61.6 MB". Closing it partway stops the download.
PDFs on reference cards can now be up to 150 MB, up from 25 MB, so a manufacturer's full price book goes on in one piece instead of split into sections.

Approving an estimate now sets its in-stock parts aside for the job. They stay on the shelf but stop counting as available, so the same parts cannot be promised to the next customer. Parts that arrive on the estimate's own order are set aside the same way.
Stock everywhere shows what is held and for which job: "0 available · 2 on hand · 2 held for jobs", with the job on hover.

The Line Items tab on an estimate and on its job shows each part as held, on order, used or short. When more stock comes in, Hold from stock sets it aside. Let go returns held parts to stock, with a reason.
Held parts are let go by themselves when the job is completed or cancelled, or the estimate is declined, expires or is replaced, and each one fitted or issued on the job comes off what is held.

Sending a purchase order to the vendor is now its own permission, "Send purchase orders to vendors", the Inventory level Edit + send orders in Roles & Permissions. Everyone who could send orders before still can. Anyone who builds estimates can still put parts on a draft order for the office to send.

Alt C (Option C on a Mac) opens your catalogs from anywhere in CrewBarn and Connect, or click the book next to search. Every PDF on your reference cards is listed, the ones you opened last at the top, and each one opens at the page you left it on. Catalogs also show up in Ctrl K search.

Page numbers in a catalog now match the printed book. When the PDF counts a cover the book does not, page 13 in the viewer is page 13 in the book, typing 13 goes there, and the tabs and Find results use the same numbers.

Order parts while you read a catalog. Press Order in the viewer, pick a vendor, then click a part number on the page, use + Order on a Find result, or type a number. It goes on a draft purchase order, and every line shows what you already have: available, on hand, on order, and on other drafts.
A part number you already carry is matched to your own item, at your cost, however the dashes are written. One you do not carry can be made into a catalog item from the order line.
Fold the order down to a bar to keep reading; it stays with you page to page and from one catalog to the next, and the next order from the same catalog goes to the same vendor.

Order from a catalog for an estimate: on the estimate's Line Items tab, press Order from a catalog. Each part goes on the estimate at its sell price and on that estimate's order only for what your shelves cannot cover. The order waits for the customer to approve, closes itself if they decline or it expires, moves to the new version if the estimate is revised, and follows the job when it becomes one.

Ordering before the customer approves takes a reason, which stays on the order. If they change their mind after it was sent, the order says so, and you can keep the parts as stock or cancel it with the vendor.
Purchase orders now show the estimate or job they are for, and each line shows its part number and the catalog page it came from.
Press / anywhere on the Product Catalog or Service Catalog to jump straight into its search box. Escape leaves it. A / typed inside another field stays where you typed it.
The Find button in a PDF on a reference card now shows its shortcut, Ctrl F (⌘F on a Mac).

Part numbers spelled out on a call now show as the number they spell. "R as in Robert, g four six zero one two two" gets a chip reading RG460122 right after the words, and "nine five four four zero, s as in Sam, nine six one zero" gets 95440S9610. Click the chip to copy it.
Phone numbers read out digit by digit show the same way, as (321) 555-1212.
The transcript itself is never changed: the words stay exactly as they were heard, and the chip sits beside them.
Vehicle and reference-card links in a note typed on an iPhone now land on the right words. An apostrophe earlier in the note used to shift them a couple of letters to the right.

Find in a PDF on a reference card: press Find, or Ctrl F, and type a part number, a model or a name. Every page is searched as you type, matches are lit up on the page, and Enter goes to the next one.
Part numbers match however they are typed: 95440S9610 finds 95440-S9610, and the other way round.
A PDF of two or three pages now opens flat, side by side, instead of a cover on its own and then the back on its own.

A PDF on a reference card now gets tabs from its own contents page when it has one. A catalogue whose contents is a table, with names down the side and sections across the top, gets a tab for each name and one for each section, coloured by section, and each opens the right page even when the printed page numbers run ahead of the file.
With no contents page, the tabs come from the headings: the biggest text on each page, ignoring the header and footer printed on every page.
Bookmarks that are only the print shop's file names are no longer used as tabs.
When there are lots of tabs, they sit across the edge with short names instead of running down it, so twenty-odd still fit and can be read.
Open Tabs in the viewer to see every set of tabs the PDF offers, and pick another if the first guess is not the one you want. Tabs you save always win.
Company settings are sorted into ten areas now. Customers & sites, Catalog & inventory and CBI AI have their own, instead of being scattered through the others.

Each area shows its settings in groups, each with an icon and one line about what it does, and the chips across the top jump to a group. Home lists every area with its groups; tap a group to land on it.
A setting page now says what it is at the top and shows the other settings in the same group, so the next thing you want is one tap away.
Reference cards are in the settings menu under Catalog & inventory › Reference. That is where you write a card and add its PDFs.
A new reference card stays open after you save it, with Add a PDF right there. Before, you had to close it and open it again to find where files go.
The links for When pay is earned, Vacation earned and Clock in and out by GPS open the right part of Shop rules. They used to open Outbound sender.
Reference cards can carry PDFs now — a manual, an install guide, a supplier's catalogue, up to 25 MB each. Add them from the card's Edit screen; they save as soon as they upload.

A PDF opens as a book rather than a long scroll: the cover on its own, then two pages side by side, and the page turns when you go forward. Arrow keys work, and so does a swipe on a phone, where it shows one page at a time.

Coloured tabs run down the edge like a printed catalogue's index tabs, and each one opens the book at its chapter. A PDF with bookmarks gets tabs straight away; open Tabs in the viewer to rename them, recolour them, or add your own at the page you are on.
Links inside the PDF work — a contents page that jumps to a section jumps there.

Files are private to your shop unless you tick that one may be shared. Even then, other shops only see it if CrewBarn approves the card for everyone, so a supplier's catalogue you keep for yourself stays yours.

The vehicle reference has a second source. Under the library's answer there is now a Lishi guide section: what the 2024 guide prints for that vehicle and year, cars and motorcycles both, with the readers, the try-out set and the page number to turn to.

Each row says whether the two sources agree. Where they do not, both stay on screen and neither is quietly swapped for the other — the vehicle in front of you settles it. Spelling is not counted as disagreement: an O printed for a zero, or the two halves of a tool written in the other order, still reads as agreeing.

Where the library had nothing, the guide fills the gap, and the card asks who on your team is carrying that tool. Vehicles the library never covered, newer models especially, now get the guide's answer instead of only No match.
When the key reference has nothing for a vehicle's year, it now just says No match instead of a paragraph about the book.

Under that, it checks your own shelf. If you have a part labelled for that vehicle, it shows with how many you hold — and one whose label names the year is marked as being for this exact vehicle rather than a near guess. Something you bought for that job beats a row from a neighbouring year.

Writing down what a vehicle takes now offers every row the card shows. It used to offer seven of the fifteen, so you could read a blank transponder number or a programming tool and had no way to record one.

You can add rows of your own, with your own titles, for anything the book has no column for. They show on the card under the book's rows, marked as yours, so nobody mistakes them for what the catalogue printed.

New: reference cards, under Files. Write down what your shop knows, pick the words that should open it, and it opens wherever those words turn up — a job description, a note, a call transcript. Nothing about it assumes a trade: it holds whatever the subject needs.

Spelling is forgiving on purpose. Write the word once and HU-101 finds HU101, SmartKey finds smart key. It stops there: one wrong character still misses, and a word never opens a card from inside a longer one, so a card on “key” stays shut on “monkey”.

Cards can have tabs. A card about a real thing gets long, and the thing somebody wanted ends up below the fold — so give it Specs, Parts, Manual, Gotchas, whatever it needs. Sections you leave untabbed sit above the tabs and stay put, because “what is this” belongs on every tab rather than hidden behind one.
You can fix a card where you found it. The Edit button is on the card itself, so a wrong line gets corrected in the job you were reading, not on a settings screen you have to go and find.
Retiring a card asks for no password and no reason, because it is undoable: it stops opening, stays in your list under Retired, and comes back whole when you bring it back.

The reference now opens down the side of the screen instead of over the middle of it. Whatever you opened it from — the transcript, the job, the message thread — stays visible beside it, which is the whole point of having a reference open.

When more than one answer fits a vehicle, those answers are tabs now rather than one stacked under the other. Only one of them is the vehicle in front of you, and stacked it was too easy to read the wrong one. The question that tells them apart sits right under the tabs.

Tool coverage now says whose list it is. The book names its own publisher's tools and is silent about everybody else's — Autel and Xhorse handle most of these vehicles — so a tool missing from the list is not a tool that cannot do the job. Those fields are editable, so you can write down what actually works for your shop.
If your inventory has a photo of a part the card names, you now see it — beside the answer, and on the shelf line. Most people recognise a part by sight long before they recognise it by number.
Vehicles named in a job description or a call transcript are now links. Click one and the key reference opens on that exact year, make and model.

The card leads with the answer that decides the job: whether a programmer is needed at all, and the one question worth asking the caller when it does. Under it are the part numbers, the tools the job names, who on your team is carrying them, and what is on the shelf.

Everything on the card can be corrected. Catalogues are wrong sometimes and the person who finds out is the tech standing at the vehicle, so an edit takes effect for your shop straight away — nobody waits on a review to get a part number that works.
A corrected value never looks like the book printed it. It is badged, and what the book said stays visible underneath, so the next person can see somebody changed it and why.

If something is wrong for everybody and not just you, tick the box when you save it and it comes to us for review. We approve it before it reaches any other shop. Your own correction keeps working whichever way that goes.
New on the Payroll page: Check before posting. It shows what the period would pay, worked out exactly the way the posted run works it out, and changes nothing.

Top of it is the warning that matters: jobs finished in this period that have never been invoiced. Those pay nobody, because a job reaches nobody’s pay until it is billed. It lists them with links so you can go and fix them — and it warns rather than blocks, so a bookkeeping gap is never why somebody is paid late.
Then every person and what they are owed: wage, commission, bonus, tips, vacation and the total, in dollars.
The figures were already being worked out — there was simply no screen, so the one check meant to happen before payroll could only happen after it.
Payroll figures now come back in dollars and cents as well as pennies. Nobody checking a pay run should have to divide 2650 by a hundred in their head to see $26.50.
The exact pennies are still there underneath and are still what the money is built from — that is what keeps it exact. The dollars are for reading.
Rounding is written down and locked: half a cent and above goes up, below it goes down. .005 favours the business, .004 favours the tech or the customer. That is the tax rule.

There is now a test that fails if anybody switches it to the other kind of rounding, the kind that sends 2.5 to 2. The two agree three times in four, so it would otherwise stay hidden until a penalty notice turned up.
A card tip has its own processing fee, and it is now kept separate from the fee on the rest of the bill.

Only the bill’s share comes off the job. $1,000 of work plus a $100 tip at 3% is a $33 fee: $30 against the job, $3 against the tip — so the profit is $970, and a tech’s commission no longer shrinks because a customer tipped them.
New setting: who carries the fee on the tip. By default the shop does and the tip is paid whole, which is how it already worked.

If you switch it to the tip, only the tip’s own share is taken — never a share of the fee on the whole bill. The screen warns that California, Maine, Massachusetts and Delaware prohibit the deduction entirely, and that federal rules bar it if it would take somebody below minimum wage.
Payslips now show what the processor took out of tips, whoever ends up carrying it.
Fixed, and this one matters: somebody who clocked hours but led no jobs got no payroll row at all. Not paid short — not paid. Anybody with hours on the clock now gets a row.
Card processing fees now come off the profit before commission, the same as parts. Paying 3% to the processor and 40% on the gross was commission on money you never had.
Tips go to the person they were left for, in full. No percentage taken, nothing deducted, and to the account on the payment rather than whoever led the job. They land in the run the payment came in.

Commission and the vacation percentage now come off the same figure, so 40% commission plus 0.05% vacation really is 40.05% of the profit on the job. Vacation used to be worked out from a number that still had the sales tax in it.

New: hourly and salaried staff bank vacation by the hour they work, instead of a percentage of a job that was never theirs. Set your days per year in Company Preferences → the default is 10, the US average after a year of service.
The screen shows what your number works out to per hour worked, so you can check it against an offer letter.
Commission is now taken from the profit on a job: everything the job sold for before tax, less what the parts cost you.
A $50 part sold at $100, a $120 service call and an hour at $95 is $315 before tax. Take off the $50 the part cost and the tech earns their percentage of $265.

Labour is not taken off. The hour on the invoice is what the job sold — deducting the wage you paid for it would shrink a tech’s commission by the amount they just earned. Only parts and a sub’s price come off.
Sales tax is out of every commission basis. It is money you hold for the state, so nobody earns a percentage of it. If a customer part-pays, only the share that was not tax counts.
A job sold under the cost of its parts pays no commission rather than a negative one. That is a job to go and fix, not a debt to take out of somebody’s wages.
The tech performance report and the payroll run now work this out the same way, so the figure you check beforehand is the figure that posts.
“Commission on a tech’s own jobs” in Company Preferences now actually does something. It had been saved and ignored, so payroll came out the same whichever way you set it.

Set it to “when the job is finished and invoiced” and commission is owed as soon as the job is billed. Set it to “when the customer has paid” and the job waits, then lands in the run the money arrived in — a job finished in March and paid in May pays in May, and only once.
The supervision bonus keeps its own separate setting, so you can bill-and-pay commission while holding bonuses until the money is in.
Separately, each person’s payroll card still sets what the percentage is taken from: what the job sold for, what was left after parts, or what the customer actually paid.

A completed job that has not been invoiced no longer pays commission. There was a case where it paid on the job’s own total, which no customer had been shown. The payroll preview already lists closed-but-unbilled jobs so you can fix them before a run.
New in Company Preferences → GPS check-in: “Only keep location during working hours”. Set the hours and the days, and anything recorded outside them is discarded.
Off by default, so nothing changes unless you turn it on.

Why it is there: background tracking runs from when a tech starts sharing until they sign out, and nobody signs out at night. The notice on their phone said “while you’re on the clock”, which was not the whole story. It now says what is actually happening, whichever way you set this.
Overnight hours work. A shift that starts on a selected day is kept through to the stop time next morning, so a Friday night crew finishing Saturday at 2am needs Friday ticked.
A phone that was out of signal all afternoon still uploads that afternoon when it reconnects in the evening — fixes are judged on when they were taken, not when they arrived.

The buttons on the incoming-call pop-up now match the rest of the app. The cream “Go to customer” was the loudest thing on the card and the second most useful, and that shade means VIP everywhere else.
Same shape, same height, same corners across every pop-up — call, message and intake. Only the fill says which button is the one to press.
The Call back button was coming out with square corners inside a rounded slot. Fixed.
Calls page rows got the same treatment, and every one of those buttons now shows a ring when you tab to it.
The equipment builder is on the web now, not just the phone — which is where the customer's spreadsheet actually is.
Paste their schedule into it and every number on the rows is kept. Describe the property instead if you have no list.
It shows what it filled in for you before you create anything, and asks when something would change the layout.
Change a draft in words — “add a roof hatch to each stair” — and the corrections you already made by hand stay put.
The equipment builder can read a pasted schedule — a spreadsheet, a hardware list, the item index off a set of drawings. Paste the rows and it keeps every number on them.

Those numbers are the point: the one stencilled on the frame and printed on the drawings is what your customer says on the phone. Describing the building as a sentence threw them away and made up labels instead.
A row with no number still gets created. Schedules have gaps, and a gap is usually something real that nobody numbered.
Reading the same schedule twice still creates it once.
The equipment builder now tells you what it filled in for you. “I assumed 2 stairwells per floor” shows above the rows, before you press create.
And it asks when something would change the layout — tap an answer and build again. At most three questions, and only ones whose answer changes the result.
You can now change a draft in words instead of starting over: “add a roof hatch to each stair”, “floor 4 has no units”. Corrections you already made by hand stay put.
If a change comes back with far fewer rows than it started with, it says so before you create.
Fixed: somebody limited to one territory was only limited on the dispatch board. They could still open and edit every job in the company from the jobs page. Territory limits now apply everywhere.
Jobs at an address no territory covers stay visible to everyone — an untagged property is nobody's ground, and hiding it means it never gets booked.
Roles can now be set to “Their territories” for job visibility: the jobs at properties in the territories assigned to them, plus their own and their team's wherever those are.
Owner and Admin always see every job. That can no longer be narrowed by a role edit or a personal override — what an admin may DO is still whatever their role grants.
Assigning yourself territories is a filter, not a limit, unless your role says “Their territories”.
New on the dashboard and the phone: My supervised projects — open work on your ground that you are not doing yourself, with how many have nobody going and how many are past due.
It stays out of your own schedule on purpose, and it does not show for anyone who already sees every job.
Jobs and estimates can now name a project manager — who is answerable for it going right, which on a bigger job is not the person turning the screwdriver.
Leave it empty and the lead tech holds it. Reassign the job and that follows, so nobody is left holding a job they are no longer on.
A project manager does not need the phone app. An office person can hold a job.
Whoever holds a job can open it, even if they are not working it — otherwise being made answerable for something means nothing.
Needs Attention now says who is answerable for each job, so you can see who to chase without opening forty of them.

Payroll can now be previewed before it posts, and the preview warns about jobs that finished in the period with no invoice on them — those pay nobody, and the warning is where the person running payroll actually is.
It warns; it never blocks. A bookkeeping gap should not be why somebody is paid late.
Jobs now record who supervised them at the moment they finish and get invoiced, so redrawing a territory later cannot rewrite who was owed what.
Supervision bonus: set a percentage per person and a foreman earns a share of the work done on his ground. It is a bonus on top of his pay, so a salaried foreman earns it too.
It pays on what the job LEFT — after parts, subcontractors, and the hours clocked on that job. Never on the cost of the job.
You choose when pay is earned, separately for commission and for the bonus: when the job is finished, or when the customer's money arrives.
A job that lost money pays no bonus and takes none back off the others.
The supervision percentage is on the payroll profile now, and the two “when pay is earned” choices are in Settings › Preferences.

On the phone, adding equipment to a job is now tick-several-then-Add. It used to add one per tap, which meant six taps were six calls to the server — slow on a bad signal, and no way to change your mind halfway.
The picker searches by the number on the thing itself, not just the name CrewBarn gave it.
It also flags anything nobody has confirmed on site, before it goes on a job.
Estimates on the phone now have an Equipment section. A quote can say which things it is for, not just what it costs — and what you name there lands on the job when the customer says yes.
Logging a part on the phone now searches your catalogue and shows what is on your own van, so you can see whether you can fit it today or it needs ordering.
You can still just type a part the catalogue has never heard of — it saves either way, and it works with no signal.
Picking a stocked part moves no stock. That still happens when the work is done.
Estimate lines on the phone can say which piece of equipment they are for, and the line list shows it. A quote covering eight items with twenty lines was unreadable without it.
Adding a product to a quote searches the catalogue the same way the job's part picker does.
You can write a note on a piece of equipment now, and it stays. The old notes box was one field that the next person to open the form wrote over; this keeps a history, dated and signed.
Notes stay with your team unless you tick “Show this to the customer” — nothing appears on the customer's page or behind a scanned label.
Techs can note an item while walking a property, straight from the list, and it works with no signal.
An item's Service history now shows what techs actually logged and noted on site, not just quotes, invoices and parts.
The baseline condition on a service plan now fills itself from the survey, so what an item was like when it came under cover is on the agreement instead of blank.
Equipment records now say whether anybody has actually seen the item. The tree builder creates items from a description, and until a tech walks the building every one of them is a guess.
An item is marked confirmed the moment a tech records its condition in the field — nothing extra to tap.
Items you already have a service log or inspection for were marked confirmed using the date of that first visit, not today's date.

Fixed: running the asset tree builder twice on a property created the whole building again — a hundred items became two hundred rows, each with its own label, and no way to tell which of a pair you were looking at.
It now skips anything already on file, matching on the name and the number the building uses.
The preview says what it would actually add before you press create: “12 new, 88 already there”.
Adding a floor later still works — only the new floor is created.
Customers can now ask up to three companies for a service plan at once, from the marketplace — a third option beside “Get an estimate first” and “Request service”.
They set the schedule as part of asking: how often, best days, time of day, months they are closed.
When you win one, it arrives in your Plan requests tab with that schedule already on it, and Start proposal builds the draft agreement from it — the same as a request made to you directly.
The other companies are marked lost automatically, as they already are for estimates.

Fixed: a paid invoice still printed “Total due $150.00” with a Scan-to-pay code under it, on a page stamped PAID. It now shows what was paid and a balance of zero, and the payment code is replaced with “Paid in full”.
That applies to your existing invoice templates as well as new ones — nothing to re-seed.

Fixed: the Bill to block was blank when no address was ticked as the customer's main one. It now falls back to their only address. A customer with one address has a main one whether or not anyone ticked the box.
Part-paid invoices now show what came off and what is left, rather than the full amount.

Fixed: emailing an invoice failed with “Class App\Services\TenantSetting not found”, on the web and in the app. A missing import — it crashed every time, and had nothing to do with the automation switch.
The red automation switch does not touch manual sends. It is only wired into the automation engine and the scheduled reminders; sending an invoice by hand was never gated.
Fixed: Receive payment said “No invoices yet” on a job whose invoice was already paid in full. It now names the invoice and says nothing is outstanding.
Portal invites had the same missing import and would have failed the same way.
“Quote the parts” on the dashboard now builds the estimate instead of dropping you on the job. It reads what the tech logged, writes one line per part needed, and opens the draft.
Every line says which item it is for — “RTU-1 — Drive belt” rather than a part number — and the lines stay in the order the tech met them walking the property.
Nothing is priced. The draft is yours to price and send.
Once quoted, those needs come off the Waiting on a quote panel, so one visit cannot be quoted twice.
Customers reading an estimate now see it grouped by item, on phone and desktop. Labour and call-out lines stay ungrouped, because they belong to the whole job.

Customers get two new tabs on your company page: Equipment — everything you have on file at their properties, when it was last serviced, and anything waiting on parts — and Service plan, showing what their plan covers and when you are next due.
Each item links to its full record rather than repeating it, so there is one set of rules about what a customer may see.
A plan's price is not shown there. That belongs on their invoices, not in a second place it can be wrong.
Techs now have a camera on every row of the walk-through, as well as inside the condition form — walking a property is look, snap, move on, and opening a form to take a picture means fewer pictures.

Customer job pages no longer show your tech's GPS coordinates or how far from the property they checked in. That is a record of where an employee was standing, and the customer is a third party to it — and "distance from site: 340m" reads as an accusation you end up explaining.
Photos you share with a customer no longer carry the coordinates of where they were taken. Your own screens still show all of it.
In its place, the customer now sees What was done: the service log for that job, item by item. Entries a tech marked internal never appear.
Techs can take photos while walking a property. They attach to the item, not the job, and queue with no signal like the rest of the walk-through.
Customers can now ask you for a service plan from their portal, and they set the schedule themselves: how often, best days, time of day, and which months they are closed.
New Plan requests tab on Service agreements, with a count of what is waiting. It shows the whole schedule they asked for, not just how often.

Start proposal builds the draft agreement with that schedule already on it — properties, covered equipment and rhythm — so nobody re-types it. The draft is unpriced and unsigned; you price it and send it.
Asking for everything at a property stays open on purpose: equipment added later is picked up when each visit is booked, rather than being frozen to the list on the day they asked.
Declining asks you for a reason, and the customer sees it.

Fixed: the Download button on Settings → Label printer showed a page of text reading "Authentication required" instead of downloading the Print Bridge. The button is fixed; nothing about your setup needs changing.
If the download cannot be fetched, the page now says so where the button is, rather than sending you to a blank page.

Techs can now take before-and-after photos while logging an item on the app, and they attach to that item rather than to the job — so they are still there a year later when somebody reads the item's own record.
Photos queue with no signal. A tech in a basement takes the picture, walks on, and it sends itself once there is a bar.
Each set has a 'Let the customer see these' switch, OFF by default. Nothing reaches the public record unless the tech ticked it.
Customer portal: a new Equipment menu, where a customer decides who can see their equipment records — another company, an inspector, or nobody. It was already built; there was no way in.
The red automation switch now pauses automatic customer emails, customer texts and external webhooks only. Staff notifications keep working.
Manual sends, incoming messages and internal work remain available. Your saved ON/OFF setting is unchanged; missed customer messages do not catch up on resume.
Improved spacing around the automation switch on Job statuses.
New dashboard panel: Waiting on a quote. Every visit where a tech logged parts that nobody has priced yet, worst first.
Each one has Quote the parts, and a link straight to that item's full record — so you can see what has already been done to it before you price more work on it.
Visits under a service plan are flagged, because they are the ones that get missed: the plan covers the visit, so the job never reaches an invoice and nothing else prompts a look.
Once something is quoted it leaves the panel. A list that keeps showing priced work is a list people stop opening.

Fixed: a scheduled visit on a property arrived with an EMPTY equipment list unless somebody had ticked items onto the agreement by hand. The tech had nothing to log against, and the visit then reported that nothing was serviced.
A plan on a property now covers what is at the property, read when the visit is booked — so equipment added in March is on the June visit without anybody remembering to add it.
If you did tick a specific list, that is still taken at its word. Three of forty means three.
Equipment you retired from a plan stays off, even if it was the only thing on the list.
Job statuses now has one red ON/OFF switch for automatic outbound emails, texts and webhooks, including staff notifications.
Manual sends, incoming messages, clocking and internal work keep working while automatic outbound is OFF. Individual automation settings are preserved.
Turning outbound automation back ON does not replay missed messages. Nothing is switched off automatically: a company administrator controls the switch.
A service plan can now say WHEN it suits the customer, not just how often: best days of the week, time of day, and months they are closed.
Visits land on a preferred day by moving forward, never earlier — turning up before you were due is its own problem.
A month they are closed pushes the visit to the day they reopen, not to the same date a month later.
The rhythm itself never drifts. "Every 3 months on a Tuesday" stays on its quarter instead of walking a few days later each visit.
When a visit is booked, the time of day rides along, so the job reaches the board with a start time instead of a gap for a dispatcher to guess at.
The incoming-call card is wider, so the caller's details and the buttons stop wrapping onto extra rows.
If the live connection drops, the card now catches up within about five seconds instead of fifteen — long enough that a ringing phone looked like nothing was happening.
A customer's equipment is now grouped by the property it is at, so "which of these is at Harbor Point" stops being something you answer by scanning a list.
Every item has a Public record link that opens exactly what somebody scanning its label would see.
Each property says when another CrewBarn company already keeps equipment records there, with a button to ask the owner for access rather than building a second list of the same equipment.
That notice appears only when there is something to say. It never names the other company or what they hold — that is what access is for.

Customers get a Service companies section in their portal: who is asking, who has access, with Allow, Decline and Take access back. Past decisions are kept so you can see you once allowed somebody, and when you stopped.
When another CrewBarn company already keeps equipment records at a property you service, the location now says so — and gives you a button to ask the property owner for access.
That is all you see until they say yes: that records exist. Not whose, not how many, not what.
The property owner decides, in their portal, not the company that built the records. They can allow, decline, set an end date, or take access back later.
Your own customers are unaffected — your equipment records are yours and always were.
Addresses are matched the way a person would read them, so "418 Riverside Ave" and "418 RIVERSIDE AVENUE" are one building. A suite number is kept, because Suite 200 and Suite 210 are not.
Existing properties need one run of Property matching in the admin maintenance panel before they can be matched.
Equipment built with the AI tree builder now gets the same A-XXXXXX code as everything else, so every label in a building looks alike and every scan link works the same way.
The numbering you typed is not lost — it becomes the item's tag, which is the number your customer's own paperwork uses.

That tag shows beside the code on the public page, on the item's record, and in an agreement's Schedule A, so somebody checking a schedule against their own equipment list recognises their own reference.
If you did not give a numbering scheme, the item simply has no tag rather than an invented one that looks like a customer reference.
A contract visit can no longer be completed while covered items have no service record. Marking one skipped with a reason is a fine answer and takes one tap; saying nothing is not.
The refusal names the items rather than just saying no, and the crew app shows the same list before the tech presses Complete.
You can switch this off per shop, but it starts on — you should not have to opt in to not misreporting what was serviced.
New Equipment tab on an agreement: everything it covers, where, when it was last serviced, what is still outstanding, and when each item joined the plan.
Equipment taken off a plan stays on the list, greyed, with the date. "We took that out in August" is exactly what somebody asks in November.
Each visit now expands to show what was done to each item, in the tech's own words.
Finishing a contract job now closes the visit it was booked for, so the plan advances and the next sweep does not book it again.
The visit records what happened to each item — done, skipped, left not working, or not there — taken from the service log, so nobody fills in a close-out screen twice.
An item with nothing logged against it is never recorded as done. A visit where four of eleven were logged says four.
It matches your own completing status by what it DOES, not what it is called, so renaming a status in settings cannot quietly break it.
The next visit's job now arrives listing what the last visit could not finish, worst first, so a part waiting since October is not found again in January.
A visit can now be issued as a report with its own number: one page per item, what was done, what was replaced, what it still needs, and the photos your tech shared.
It reads from the service log, so nobody retypes anything. A part still waiting on approval says exactly that — never what it was quoted at.
Like every report, it is frozen when you issue it. Work logged on a later visit does not change a report the customer already has.
Internal notes never reach it, even if the report was built from a list that included one.
An item the owner has marked private drops off the public copy, and the page says how many were left out.
A visit spread over two days now says so instead of showing the first day only.
Service agreements now carry a Schedule A: every covered item by ID, what it is, where, which service and how often — each ID linking to that item's record.
An item you have marked private shows only its ID and name on the schedule. No maker, no model, no location. Nobody gets a shopping list out of a document you emailed.
Retiring an item takes it off the next schedule you send. It stays in the agreement's history.
Contract terms — notice to cancel, response time, labour and after-hours rates, parts discount — fall back to your shop defaults and can be overridden per agreement.
Terms you have not set print as a visible blank if the agreement needs them, and drop out entirely if they are optional, so you never send a sentence with a hole in it.
When AI drafts an agreement it is now editing a real base document built from your trade, and the draft is refused if it drops the schedule, types an equipment ID, or invents a price or a date.
On Add missing templates, the starters that have updates now have a Review them now button instead of telling you to go and find another button.
Two new agreement templates: Repair agreement for a one-visit job, and Project agreement for phased work with milestone payments. Both fill themselves in from the job and its approved estimate.
An agreement lists the equipment the job covers, each with its ID and a link to its record, so a year later you can prove what was in scope.
Terms you settle once with your lawyer — warranty length, late fee, deposit percentage, insurance limit, your state and any required notices — now live in settings instead of being retyped per job.
A deposit is worked out to the exact cent, and the agreement states the balance. With no deposit set, it simply says payment is due on completion.
Anything you have not filled in prints as a blank line rather than a guess. A made-up warranty length reads exactly like an agreed one, so we never invent them.
Agreements are their own kind of document now, so Send agreement offers agreements and not job sheets.
Scanning a label now shows what was actually done to that piece of equipment: every visit, grouped by the day and the tech who came, with what they did, what they replaced and what it still needs.
Photos a tech marks as shareable show on that record, labelled before and after. Nothing is published unless somebody ticks it.
Equipment on a service plan says so on its public page, with how often it is visited and when the next visit is due. Never what the plan costs.
The owner controls each part separately. The work history, the photos and the plan details can each be switched off without hiding the rest of the record.
A property's groups now say how many items were serviced recently and how many need attention, instead of only how many there are.
Fixed: invoice, work-order and estimate templates always printed a second page, even when the whole document was one line. There was a forced page break sitting in front of the line items.
Fixed: the signature line on seeded agreements printed a stray bit of code where a dash should be. If your templates are unedited, Starter wording in the admin maintenance panel corrects them.
Fixed: an item's public page could fail to load entirely if a photo link could not be built. The words load now and the picture is simply left out.
A part a tech flagged now follows its quote by itself: approved when the customer approves, and closed when somebody logs fitting it. Nobody has to update the item's record by hand.
A repair job made from a parts quote now arrives with the equipment already on it, so the tech has something to log against.
Turning a quote down leaves the item still saying it needs the part — it just stops anyone chasing a quote that was declined.
Fitting one part closes one need. Two of the same part flagged on one item are still two parts.

Parts a tech finds on a maintenance visit can now be quoted in one press. It builds a separate estimate — the visit itself stays covered by the plan — with a line per part, each attached to the item it is for.
The quote reads worst first, so a safety item is at the top rather than wherever it happened to be typed.
A part cannot end up on the bill twice, however many times the button is pressed.
If the customer's plan includes a parts discount it comes off automatically, to the exact cent.
A new Parts needed list shows everything outstanding across every job, worst first — the question no single job can answer.

A private label is no longer a dead end for the person who owns the building. Scanning one now offers “Is this your building? Sign in with portal login” — the same login they use for their invoices, no second account.

Signed in, they see everything on their own equipment with no code and no expiry, and a green bar says whose account they are in with a way to sign out. The same browser might be a contractor’s tomorrow.
Their whole property reads as theirs, so the list beside an item they are reading no longer shows a private label on equipment they own.
Somebody given access to one item still gets one item. Being let into one item is not being let into the building.
Nothing changes for anyone scanning off the street.
Your customers can now see their own equipment. Signed into the portal, scanning one of their own private items shows the whole record — no access code, no 24-hour expiry. It is their building.
They control who else gets in: give someone access to one item, an area or a whole property, with or without an end date, and take it back the moment they want to.
Every look at a private record is written down — who, when, and how they were entitled to — and the owner can see that list.
Nothing changes for anyone scanning a sticker off the street; they see exactly what they saw before.
Who approves an access request is now a setting. Your workspace keeps deciding exactly as it does today unless you hand it to the customer.

Fixed: the public page for a piece of equipment was showing estimate numbers, whether the estimate was approved, and the wording of billing lines — to anyone who scanned the sticker. A competitor standing in front of it could see what you had quoted for it.
Public asset pages now show only what was done to the thing: parts fitted with their serial, and inspection verdicts. No quotes, no job billing lines, no counts of either.
A test now walks every public page and fails on anything that looks commercial, so this cannot come back by accident.

You can now issue one report for a whole property instead of handing somebody forty separate ones. It has its own number, one verdict for the building, and a single list of what needs fixing across every item — most urgent first, each line saying which item.
The verdict is the worst item, not an average. Thirty-nine sound ones do not offset the one that has failed.
The report is frozen when you issue it. An inspection done next week does not change a report you handed over today, which is what makes it usable as evidence.
Rolling up a property inspected every quarter shows its current state — the latest inspection of each item, not the same item four times.
Private items are left out rather than blocking the whole report, and the page says how many were withheld.
You can record who was given a copy, so 'did the fire marshal ever get it' is not somebody's memory.
