Everything a report says needs fixing is now a tracked item with a deadline, instead of a line on a document nobody can act on. Life-safety issues are due the same day, 30-day items thirty days from the inspection, and the rest by the next visit.
Quote the fixes builds one estimate with a line per outstanding item, each attached to the item it is for — so nothing gets missed retyping the list.
The report itself says where each fix got to: Quoted, Approved, Fixed, or Waived. A customer reading it a month later stops chasing work already in hand.

An item past its fix-by date now shows the asset as overdue on its public page, even if the next inspection is not due for months. An inspection being in date says when something was last looked at, not that it is in order.
Waiving something needs a reason, and it stays on the record.
Inspection and service reports now have a page a customer can open: the verdict in plain words, what needs fixing with a date against each one, and everything that was checked.
Each finding says why it matters, not just what is wrong — so a property manager can tell a torn smoke seal from a missing sign without calling you.
Every report gets a number like R-26-00418 that somebody can read off paper and type in to check the report is genuine. It is on the page next to a Verify button.
Reports for items marked private are not published. The page says the owner keeps it private and shows nothing else — not the name, not the findings.
The page prints properly, because inspectors carry paper.
Job statuses now use the available page width and group active statuses into Not started, Working, Waiting and Done. The main menu stays in place.
Switch between Stages and Rules, see tech-app actions and Ready to invoice badges, and add a status directly to its stage. Existing editors remain available.
This release changes presentation only. It does not activate customer messages, change delivery settings, or add drag-and-drop yet.

Already have the agreement on paper? Upload the signed contract on a new service agreement and CrewBarn reads the services, how often each one happens, the fee and the term off it — then fills the form in for you to check.
It will not guess. Anything the contract does not actually say comes back blank and is listed as something you have to fill in, because a made-up billing day reads exactly like an agreed one.
The customer and the properties are never matched for you. It shows you what the contract says and you pick the records yourself.
Nothing is saved until you walk through all four steps and press the button, the same as an agreement you typed in by hand.

Fixed: Draft one for me has never actually drafted anything. It was calling a piece of code that does not exist, and the failure looked exactly like the AI being unavailable — so it quietly handed back the generic starter contract every time.

A service can now list the equipment it covers — the actual units, gates or machines — ticked from the properties on the agreement. A year later the record says which of the eleven were serviced, instead of just a job title.
When a visit goes on the board, its job arrives carrying only the equipment at that property. A visit to one building does not turn up with another building's equipment on it.

Fixed: attaching equipment to a job has never actually worked. The permission rule behind it referred to a setting the app does not use, so every attempt was refused with nothing on screen to say so. It works now, on jobs and estimates too.

The customer box on a new agreement is wider, and long names in the search results wrap instead of being cut off. Two customers whose names differed only past the cut both showed as the same thing, which made picking between them a guess.

How often is a plain list now — Every week, Every 2 weeks, Every month, Every 3 months, Once a year — instead of a box with a number in it. “Every 1 month” read like the 1 might be a day. Anything unusual is still possible under Custom.
Each service has a What this involves box. It goes into the agreement, so the customer reads what they are actually buying instead of just a service name.

Setting up a service agreement is four short steps now — who it is for, what you will do, the money, and the paperwork — instead of one long page. You can jump back to any step from the row at the top.
Beside it, a panel that fills in as you go: how many jobs the agreement books in its first year, what it bills, each service's visit count, and the dates of the first visits.

Those numbers come from the same scheduler that will actually book the work, so what you see before you agree is what you get after. A quarterly lock service and seasonal grounds care at one property previews as 46 jobs and $7,200 — and creates exactly that.
Service agreements can be signed now. Send to sign emails the customer a link; when they sign, the agreement starts itself and the visit dates go on straight away.
They signed on paper does the same thing for the ones signed at a kitchen table, which is most of them.
The wording is frozen the moment you send it, so editing the document afterwards cannot change what the customer signed.
Before the four pages, the customer sees a short summary of what they are agreeing to: what is covered, how often, the fee and the term.
While it is waiting to be signed it books nothing and bills nothing, and the page says so.

A service agreement now has tabs: Overview, Visits, Billing and History. All of it was already being recorded and none of it was on screen — so you could not see when you are next there, whether they have paid, or what has happened.
Overview shows the next five visits with the property and whether each is on the board yet, and what has been billed, paid and what is next.
Visits lists the whole year with a link to the job each one became. Billing lists every period with its invoice. History reads in plain sentences instead of event codes.

The status says what it means: Not started, Running, Paused — with a line telling you that a not-started or paused agreement books no visits and bills nothing. Start it and Pause are right there, and starting one places its dates straight away.
A job booked by a service agreement now says so at the top, in green: covered, do not collect payment for the visit, with a link to the agreement.
Its invoice button reads Invoice extra work, and asks you once before it goes ahead — so billing a covered visit is a decision rather than an accident.

Draft one for me now writes a real agreement instead of a few generic lines. It is told what you just set up — the customer, the properties, each service and how often it happens including the seasonal changes, the fee and the term — and writes them into the wording.
You get eleven proper sections, and a table of the services with their real rhythms.

Two lists you can edit before it writes: what is included in the fee, and what is charged separately. They come pre-filled with what is true of any plan, and they become their own sections in the agreement — the ones every argument about a service plan is really about.
Nothing is invented for something you did not say. Anything unanswered stays a blank for you or your lawyer, because a made-up notice period reads exactly like an agreed one.

Jobs booked by a service agreement now say so, and CrewBarn stops you invoicing one twice. The fee already covers the visit — pressing Invoice job on it used to charge the customer a second time with nothing on screen to warn you.
If the tech found extra work on a covered visit you can still bill for that: you are asked once, told which agreement covers the visit, and then it goes through.

The customer box on a new service agreement is a search now, not a list of every customer you have. Type a name or account number. There is a + New customer button beside it if they are not in there yet, and their first property is ready to tick without a reload.

One agreement can now cover more than one service. Servicing the locks every quarter and cutting the grass weekly in summer and every other week in winter is ONE agreement with two services — add them with + Add another service, and each keeps its own rhythm and seasons.

New agreements can be started, not just saved. Until now everything you created sat as a draft, and a draft books no visits, no jobs and no invoices — so nothing you set up ever happened. Start the agreement puts it live and places the visit dates straight away; Save as a draft still leaves it parked.
You can say who looks after an agreement. They get the renewal reminders, and they are the lead on any job it books that has no tech of its own.
Job type no longer quietly defaults on every new service, which is how everything ended up booking the first kind of job in your list.

How often now reads the way you would say it: “Normally every week”, then “But from November to March, every 2 weeks”. Underneath, it writes the whole schedule back to you as a sentence — so you can read what you are about to promise instead of working it out from dropdowns.
The everyday rhythm can no longer be deleted by accident, which used to leave an agreement that only visited in winter.
No more “every 1 months”.
The old four-field new-contract box is gone. Everything goes through the full form, which asks for the properties and the service as well.
Drafting a contract now shows you what it wrote. It used to close the box and quietly attach the thing — you never saw the document. You get it on screen, then Attach it or Open and edit.

Tool Shed → Service Agreements can write your terms into the agreement instead of leaving blanks. Tell it what you cover, what you do not, your cancellation and payment terms, and those go into the wording. Anything you leave empty stays an honest blank — nothing is invented.

New: upload the agreement you already use — a PDF or a photo of the paper copy — and CrewBarn reads it into an editable draft, turning the per-customer parts into fill-ins. Read it against the original before you use it; it is a machine reading your paperwork. Needs AI switched on.

How often now takes as many rhythms as the work really has — weekly all year, every two weeks November to March, quarterly, whatever it is. A season can run backwards through the year end, and where two overlap the seasonal one wins. You no longer have to say “every 1 month” and fix it on the next screen.
The new service agreement form is full width with the same header as New Job, instead of a narrow column.
Maintenance contracts is now called Service agreements throughout, and New contract takes you to the full form rather than the four-field one.
The new service agreement form now shows each property's actual address instead of “Unnamed property”, and looks like the rest of CrewBarn.
You can attach the contract the customer signs, right on the form — pick one you already have, or press Draft one for me and CrewBarn writes it while you wait.

That opens over the form rather than sending you somewhere else, with the plain warning that CrewBarn is not a law firm and a lawyer needs to read it before you send it. You get an editable draft, switched off until you turn it on.
Service agreements is now one of the areas you can switch off in Modules, like Warranties or Subcontracting. Off means it disappears from your menus — nothing you have already agreed is touched.

Fixed: the new service agreement links did not appear for anyone using the Easy layout — which has its own menus, and had never heard of contracts. Jobs now lists Service agreements and New service agreement alongside the rest, and there is a + Service Agreement button next to + New Job.
Service agreements have their own form now, and you can start one from wherever you happen to be: the + button, the Jobs tab, the Estimates tab, or straight off a property on a customer's record.
Starting one from a property fills the customer and that address in for you.

The form asks for the whole thing in one go — who it is for, which properties, what you will do and how often, the fee and the term. The old one asked for four fields and no service, which produced an agreement that looked signed and did nothing, because a service with no rhythm never books a visit.
Pick several properties and each one gets its own visit and its own job, which the form tells you as you tick them.

New page: Tool Shed → Service Agreements. CrewBarn can now write you a service agreement to start from — the wording a customer signs before you begin work on a schedule. It comes out as an ordinary draft document you can edit, preview and send.
It could do this before, but there was nowhere to click. The page is the part that was missing.

Before it writes anything you read what CrewBarn is and is not doing, and type that you understand. CrewBarn is not a law firm, and a generated agreement needs a lawyer's eye before it goes to a customer — that note is printed on the document itself, so it survives being emailed or exported.
You can record who reviews your agreements, so the draft has somewhere to go. If you do not have anyone yet, the page suggests the kinds of place worth trying and why.

There is a slot for their API key, stored encrypted. Nothing sends to it yet — no legal service is connected to CrewBarn and we are not going to pretend otherwise. It is there so that when there is one worth using, your key is already where it belongs.

Contracts now write next year's agreement for you. As one comes up for renewal you get the next term ready to read — same services, same rhythms, same properties, starting the day the old one ends — with the price already at whatever increase you set.
It arrives as a draft, so you can change the price or anything else before you activate it. A contract set to renew automatically goes live on its own instead, so the billing never stops.
There is a Renew button's worth of it on demand too, if you would rather not wait for the overnight run.
The increase applies to the line rates as well as the overall fee, so the two do not drift apart.

A renewal is a new agreement linked back to the one it replaces, rather than the old one having its dates pushed out. Last year's prices, invoices and visits stay attached to last year, so you can still see what you charged.
A contract set to renew automatically that had already run past its end now gets picked up and renewed, instead of sitting there looking live while billing nothing.
Fixed: the renewal price could come out a cent low on certain increases — $1.00 at 2.5% worked out to $1.02 instead of $1.03.

Two new things you can build an automation on: a contract coming up for renewal, and a contract running out. Pick them in the automation builder like any other moment — email the customer their agreement is due, tell the office when one lapses, whatever suits.
How far ahead the renewal notice goes out is set per contract, so a big agreement can warn you three months out while a small one warns you a week out.
Contract wording now fills in properly on those messages — the agreement's name, its dates, what it covers and the fee. They would otherwise have gone out with those spots blank.

A contract whose term has ended now moves itself to Expired instead of sitting in your list looking live while doing nothing. One set to renew automatically is left alone rather than being closed behind your back.
No new visit reminder, on purpose: contract visits become ordinary jobs, and your job reminders already cover those. Adding another would have messaged the customer twice about the same visit.

New setting: whether contract invoices wait for you. Contracts raise their own invoices when each billing period starts — you can now have those count straight away instead of sitting as drafts for somebody to open. Tool Shed → Whether contract invoices wait for you.
Off to begin with, so nothing changes on your books unless you ask. With fifty agreements that is fifty invoices a month to open, which is what the switch is for.
Either way nothing is emailed to a customer. Sending an invoice is still something you do.
If anything goes wrong counting one, it falls back to a draft you can issue with one click rather than being lost, and the contract's history says what happened.

Fixed, and it affects ordinary invoices too: issuing an invoice now records it in your books in the same single step. Before, if the bookkeeping entry failed the invoice still went out as issued with nothing behind it — a gap you would only find at the end of the quarter.

Contracts can now bill on a set day of the month. Put 1 in Billing day and every contract invoices on the 1st, whatever date it was signed — so a customer with several agreements gets them together instead of scattered through the month.

The short first stretch is charged by the day, not as a whole period. A contract signed on the 20th that bills on the 1st pays for those twelve days of the month and no more, and the invoice line says “part period” so the smaller figure explains itself.
The same goes at the other end: a contract that finishes mid-month is only charged to the day it finishes.
A part stretch that works out to nothing does not raise an invoice at all.

Monthly contracts only — a day of the month does not mean anything to a weekly one, so those still run from the date the contract started. And a billing day of 31 falls on the 30th in a month that has no 31st, rather than skipping.

Maintenance contracts now raise their own invoices. Every period that has begun gets a draft invoice for the contract fee, with the dates it covers written on the line — the visits themselves are never invoiced separately, because the fee already covers them.
They arrive as drafts, not as something already sent. Nothing reaches a customer until you open the invoice and issue it.

A period is billed once and only once. Two runs at the same moment cannot both raise it, and a run that fails part way leaves no half-made invoice behind — the period simply stays owed and is tried again.
Tax follows the contract if you have set one on it, otherwise the customer's usual rate, otherwise your shop's default.
A contract signed with a start date well in the past catches up a year at a time rather than filling your invoice list in one go, and tells you how many periods are still to come.
Fortnightly and weekly agreements bill correctly. Two periods inside one month are two invoices — an earlier version could only record one a month and would have quietly billed those customers short.

Maintenance contract visits now turn into real scheduled jobs on their own. Anything due in the next two weeks lands on the board and in the tech app like any other job, with the right kind of work, the right property and the line's tech already on it.
A job keeps the date the visit was due, not the day it was created — so a visit picked up late still reads as the day it was meant to happen.
A visit becomes a job once and only once. It cannot be booked twice even if two runs overlap, so nobody gets sent to work somebody has already done.

If one service cannot be booked — its kind of job has been deleted, say — that visit alone is skipped and stays waiting for the next run. The rest of the week still gets booked, and the reason is written to the contract's log.
Contracts now has a menu entry, under Work. The pages were there but you had to know the address.

Maintenance contracts now place their visit dates. Each service books its own schedule at each property, and where a rhythm changes with the season the dates follow it — the step is always taken from the last visit, so the turn of a season never doubles a visit or leaves a gap.

Run it as often as you like: a second run fills forward from the last visit rather than starting again, and places nothing if there is nothing left to place. Nothing becomes a job or an invoice at this stage.
Platform admin can preview a tenant's schedule without writing anything.
New section: Maintenance contracts. Work you have agreed to do on a schedule, with each service on the contract keeping its own rhythm.

A rhythm can change with the season. Every week April to October and every other week November to March is one service, not two contracts. The year is drawn across twelve months so you can see the seasons meet — and it tells you if they don't, naming the month nothing covers.
Each service books its own kind of job, so different trades land on the board as different work rather than one blurred “maintenance”.

Generating a service agreement now asks you to acknowledge, once, that CrewBarn is not a law firm and the result needs a lawyer's eye before you send it. It suggests where to take it, and the draft carries the note on the document itself.
Templates & forms has a new stage on the Journey board: On contract. Maintenance agreements get their own moments — contract signed, visit coming up, visit report — alongside the job ones.
Four new starter templates to go with them: a maintenance agreement with the covered services and how often each one happens, a visit report, and a visit reminder by email and text.
New things you can put on a document: the contract name, its term, who supervises it, what it covers and how often, the fee and how it is billed, and the next visit date.

Forms built with Make a form now leave out a field that does not apply, instead of printing its code. A statement for a customer with no parent account used to read “Sub-customer name: {{sub_customer.name}}” — on the document the customer receives. The label goes with it.
Date of service now sits in the header on work orders and receipts, where it is a real line, rather than being described as a column of a table that only statements have.

New: Make a form. Pick a form you know, tap the fields you want on it, choose a colour and a name, and it builds a branded document — with a live preview the whole way and no merge tags to learn. Find it on Templates & forms.
Fixed: whatever you had selected — a view, a channel filter, a tab — was drawn as an empty white box with the label invisible. A colour used in ten places across CrewBarn had never been defined.
Fixed: filtering the journey board to Documents hid every document you had written yourself. Your own templates now filter along with everything else instead of disappearing.

Job stages and By channel now speak the same language as the rest of the page: green means it sends, and status reads "In use" or "Off" instead of a dot you had to decode. The raw merge-tag column is gone — it was code, on the one page that promises you never have to read it.

Two new things you can put on a document: the customer's Account #, and the Sub-customer name — the unit or property the work was done for, when that customer sits under a parent account. The parent (who gets billed) and the sub-customer (where the work happened) can now both appear on the same statement line.

Templates & forms now opens on the Journey board for everyone. If you had used the page before, it kept showing you whichever view you last had — so the new one was there but you never landed on it. You still get all four views; the switch is under the heading.
Fixed the view switch sitting on top of the Draft with AI and New template buttons on the job-stages view.
The update card no longer asks you to reload for changes and then list none. When a release has no notes of its own it shows the most recent ones instead, labelled as such.

New template now asks what the moment is and how it goes out before what to start from — and if you already have one for that moment, it says so and offers to open it instead of quietly adding a second. Start from CBI, CrewBarn's version, a copy of one of yours, or blank.
Fixed: two updates could share a version number, and when that happened the update card hid one of them — so notes were written that nobody could read.

Templates & forms has a List view: every template once, with the moment it belongs to and what the customer sees first. Copies fold into their template and show as a count, so the list never repeats the same thing five times. Search looks inside the message, not just the name, and there is a Show archived toggle.

Fixed: statement templates could not be previewed at all. Opening Preview — or picking Sample data — asked you to choose a job billed to a commercial customer and stopped there, which is impossible when you are just laying the form out. It now shows sample figures and says so, and still uses the real account balances when you pick a qualifying job.

Templates & forms opens on a new Journey board: one card per moment a customer hears from you, in the order a job actually happens, with a chip per channel showing whether it sends, is switched off, or does not exist yet. Pick any moment to see what the customer gets. The job-stage and by-channel views are still there — the switch is at the top right.

Fixed the duplicate templates. Renaming a template made CrewBarn stop recognising it, so the next "Add missing CrewBarn templates" added the original back — again and again. Separately, seeding could re-add the entire library in one go, which is where the runs of five identical names came from. Both are fixed, so no new copies will appear.

For the copies you already have: a banner now says how many there are, and "Clean them up" puts the versions side by side so you choose which one customers get. The rest are archived, not deleted, and can be brought back.
Fixed an editor showing [object Object] instead of your message when the content came from AI, a starter, or an extracted design.
Required custom fields appear below the document shortcuts and above Job Basics. Optional custom fields remain below Line Items. Required includes fields required on the form or before invoicing.
Job Custom fields now appear directly below the document shortcuts and above Job Basics, open by default, so customer-specific VIN, PO and WO fields are easier to find.

Fixed: turning on a customer's monthly statement stopped you saving that customer at all. Any edit — phone number, address, payment terms — came back "not authorized" with nothing to say why. Ordinary edits now save normally while statements are running. Changing the statement's own day, recipients or subject still asks you to pause it first, and now says so instead of failing silently.

Creating a job from a call for someone who is not a customer yet now needs permission to add customers, not just to create jobs. It makes a customer record, so it asks for the same permission that adding one by hand does.

Custom-field saves now notify open forms to reload field definitions without a page refresh. Create, edit, activate, deactivate and delete changes use a tenant-scoped event, not periodic polling. Returning to the tab also checks for changes; entered values stay intact.

Job custom fields can now be included in invoice email subjects and at the top of invoice email bodies, following the selected-customer rules. Missing subject values block sending. Customer subjects already using the field tag are not duplicated.
The template builder now lists statement table, total due and currency tags. Default value help explains why VIN, PO and WO defaults should usually stay blank.
Customer Tax & Billing now puts Statement send day directly below payment terms, with a link to choose the customer's statement template. Unsaved changes are checked before leaving.
Customer Templates now includes Create templates in Connect, opening in a separate tab. Automatic statement sending remains off.

Customer statements: set a monthly day, recipients and subject under customer Tax & Billing. Open the saved customer, then Records → Invoices → Preview statement for the PDF pack, delivery history and monthly enable/pause controls. Fixed the enable/pause request. Automatic sending remains off system-wide.

Statement packs put the statement first, followed by unpaid invoices including overdue balances, without changing NET due dates. Customer-specific fields and invoice email subjects support references such as PO and WO; statement templates are available per customer.

CBI photo research uses web research before checking inventory and offers possible matches, not confirmed fitment. Photo guidance adapts to the subject; locksmith VIN research uses decoded vehicle details for possible keys.

Call recordings now play from CrewBarn's own storage instead of fetching from the phone provider every time. They load faster, they keep working after the provider's temporary link expires, and they are still there when the provider's retention window closes.

Fixed recordings not downloading in the phone app. The app was being redirected to the provider and the hand-off failed there; it now gets the audio from CrewBarn directly. This also stopped the app's login token being passed to the phone provider on every play.
Recordings from before this change are pulled across in the background, oldest first.

Teach CBI now shows the photos that came WITH the request you are looking at, not every photo that customer has ever sent. A dealer who texts you every week was stacking months of unrelated pictures above the one being taught. Photos sent within half an hour of the request stay together, so a picture and the message describing it are not split up. “Show the whole conversation” is still one click away.
The intake approval text now appears in the customer's thread, so their reply of APPROVED sits under the question instead of arriving on its own.

New contact checkbox: Approves intake. When someone texts work to your intake number, the contacts you tick get a text from that same number saying who sent it and what they asked for, with “Reply APPROVED to authorize it”. Their reply marks the intake approved and records their name against it. Nothing is scheduled by a text — someone still opens the queue and turns it into a job.
The wording is yours to change: Templates now includes “Intake approval request (text)”.

Approves intake is separate from Intake / bill-to on purpose. Bill-to says which customer an incoming number belongs to; Approves intake says whose yes counts. The front desk that sends the work is often not the person who signs for it.
Fixed: when two customers shared a phone number, an incoming intake could be attributed to either of them and not always the same one. It now resolves the same way every time.

New under Inventory Settings: Lock the store. Off (how it works today) a tech scans any part straight onto their van. On, only the staff you give Edit inventory to can move stock — they transfer it to a tech's van and the tech scans each item in to confirm they got it. Scanning still does the moving either way; this decides who gets to decide.
Under lock, a tech scanning something nobody sent them is told to ask the office rather than being left guessing, and the app counts down how many are left on the transfer as they scan.
A transfer that is part-scanned can no longer also be accepted in one go — that would have moved the same items twice. Whoever starts scanning finishes scanning.

Techs can load their own van. Settings → My stock shows what is on board with targets and what is short, and Check in scans parts straight on — the camera stays open so a whole pile goes on in one go. Nobody at the shop has to raise a transfer or approve it: the QR label is on one physical item and cannot be scanned without holding it, so the scan itself records what moved and where it came from.
Transfer requests are still there for the other case — asking for something you do not have in your hand, which a scan cannot do.

Vans and shelves can be told what they should carry. Inventory → Stock has a new “Should carry” column and field: set the number a van or shelf is meant to hold and it shows “short 3” the moment it drops below. Leave it blank and that spot is not stocked with the item on purpose — nothing reports it as short. Blank and 0 are different: 0 means it should carry none.

Techs get My van stock in the app: what their own truck is short of, worst first, with an Ask button that requests the restock from the shop. The old low-stock list adds every location together, so a van could be empty while the shop held fifty and nothing looked wrong.

Fixed: techs could not raise, accept, reject or cancel a stock transfer request, even though the whole point of the request is that the truck's tech consents to stock arriving or leaving. Who may act on a transfer is unchanged — only the person it is addressed to can accept or reject it, and accepting still means scanning each unit.

A tech is never blocked from using a part that is in front of them. Shop stock, warehouse stock, their own van or another tech's van all go on the job — every stocked item carries a QR fingerprint and has to be scanned, so CrewBarn already records which physical unit was used, where it came from, who took it and which job it went on.

New under Inventory Settings: Watch van stock. With it on, a tech using a part out of another tech's van raises a transfer request to put one back from the shop, addressed to the van's tech to confirm when it arrives. Several parts off the same van become one request, not several.

Vans and shelves can now be told what they are supposed to carry. If the tech who took the part is set to carry that part on their own van, the restock request says so — their van was empty when it should not have been.

Tool Shed dropdown now lists permitted tools alongside Connect, respecting module and settings access. Fixed overflowing toolbar view switches. Job and estimate descriptions search products and services as you type. CBI navigation groups training, skills and setup.

CBI can find a call without you knowing whose it is. Ask for a person, a business name, an account number or a phone number in any format, and it searches all of them; if the name is not a customer it looks for it inside the call transcripts instead, and tells you that is what it did. When one name matches two customers it now says so rather than answering about whichever came first.
Ask CBI for the words spoken on a call — "find the call about the broken deadbolt" — and it searches the transcripts themselves.

New Messages permission under Roles & Permissions. It opens the company message inbox and is on for owners and admins; turn it on for other roles as you like. Reading the messages on a job you are assigned to is unchanged and needs nothing new.
Folder tabs now use aligned cards with slim status-color accents, clearer selection and stable hover behavior.

Route History includes active staff with app access, not only field technicians. Replay shows clickable job dots for the selected person's scheduled jobs overlapping the date and hour window, with customer names and links to job details. Existing viewing permissions still apply.

CBI skills now separate available training from planned responsibilities with distinct icons and counts. Invoice learning has a dedicated screen showing saved source settings and direct access to invoice-sourced knowledge; it does not enable automatic billing.

Teach CBI now explains hands-on training, supervised drafts and the remaining independent-task work in a three-stage overview. Connection setup collapses when configured to leave more room for training.

Review conversation photos without closing CBI: use Previous, Next or thumbnails. Teaching notes show saved/unsaved state, an Undo option and a character count. Switching photos or closing asks before discarding edits; saving locks navigation until complete.
Drag zoomed CBI photos with your mouse to pan in any direction. Grab/grabbing cursors show when panning is available. Touch scrolling and scrollbars remain available.

CBI photo details can look up manufacturer phone numbers and addresses with a cited source and lookup date. Confirm the manufacturer name before searching. Requires an active Anthropic connection; missing or unsourced contact details are not guessed.

CBI photo details now include zoom up to 4x, contrast adjustment and Reset. Scroll or swipe around enlarged photos while keeping AI details and teaching notes alongside. Adjustments do not change the original image.

Conversation photos now have a clickable AI badge that opens the photo, AI description, suggested match and teaching notes together. Removed the separate stack of photo teaching boxes. Editing still requires Teach CBI permission; multi-photo message analysis is clearly labeled.

Staff can receive separate Company Info and Shop Rules access. Hidden and view-only choices are enforced by the API and shared Connect navigation. Reminder and automation changes, including test-send, now require edit access and respect Shop Rules restrictions. Workspace tool visibility no longer depends on permission to read Shop Rules.

Warranty settings now support employee-specific hidden, view-only and edit access, with separate API read/write checks. Staff uses the same access selector for Modules and Warranty settings. Existing broad access is preserved until explicitly overridden.

Modules is the first setting with explicit employee access: follow settings permissions, hidden, view only, or edit. Modules editing is enforced by the API; navigation configuration remains readable by staff so workspace menus can render. Requires matching API and frontend deployment.
View-settings staff can inspect Modules. Presets, switches and saving require Edit settings, matching existing API protection.
Sidebar and mobile Tool Shed menus now share the main menu's visibility rules, including workspace settings placement. Navigation uses the precise module keys instead of legacy grouped names.

Staff personal permissions now include clear area-level selectors for no view/edit access, view only, or view and edit. These use existing role overrides and API permissions; special actions remain separately controlled. Individual-setting permissions are not yet available.

Disabled Franchise and communication modules now stay out of desktop and mobile navigation. Quick-create links and the CBI header follow module visibility, failed refreshes no longer overwrite saved module settings, and Connect waits for a confirmed access decision.

Invoice AI learning can now compare billed work with up to 20 explicitly job-linked messages and their human photo teaching notes. Existing AI and invoice-learning settings still apply. Photos and storage URLs are not sent; unrelated customer conversations are excluded.
Each dashboard module now has a distinct, recognizable icon in the same consistent style: dispatch, invoices, inventory, payroll, staff, CBI and more. Module settings and behavior are unchanged.

Conversation photos now have per-photo finish and AI teaching notes for staff with Teach AI permission. Notes do not confirm a catalog match, and memory creation follows existing learning settings. Requires the matching API update. Invoice-to-conversation learning is not included yet.

Crew right now now uses the newest GPS fix instead of letting an old live event override newer server data. GPS refreshes every 30 seconds as a fallback; the header shows the last successful check rather than a live clock.

Intake now has a read-only newer-customer-messages panel. It shows up to 20 inbound messages after the source message from the same conversation, without marking them read or changing a job. Replies still require human review.

Saved intake follow-ups can now be reviewed in their original conversation and explicitly loaded into the message composer. Recipient and conversation checks precede loading; nothing sends automatically. Existing composer text and attachments require confirmation before replacement.

Missing-details drafts can now be saved with the intake without sending. Revision checks reject stale overwrites, and saving records an audit event. New AI extraction cannot overwrite a saved human follow-up draft. Requires the latest API.

Intake now includes a manual missing-details draft helper: choose questions, edit wording, copy it and open the original conversation. Nothing sends automatically, and drafts are not saved when you leave the intake view.
Human intake-to-job approval now records the reviewer and linked job in durable training history. The approval record shares the job transaction, so an audit failure rolls back the database changes.

Intake review history now records durable before/after details for ordinary edits and dismissals. An audit failure rolls back the review change. These records do not teach a lasting rule or grant CBI authority.

Intake teaching history now includes durable before/after parts corrections and saved lessons alongside photo teaching. Audit failures roll back the correction and lesson together. Earlier corrections are not backfilled.

CBI setup now saves the AI master switch separately from provider settings, warns before resuming enabled tasks, and shows unsaved switch changes. Connection-test results are hidden when their tested form values change.

CBI AI now shows an activation checklist with direct links to provider setup, the AI master switch and Modules. Saved configuration is distinguished from a live connection test, and hiding CBI from menus is distinguished from pausing AI tasks.

Teach CBI photos: Measure & identify adds human-calibrated ruler measurements, inch/metric conversion and physical diameter/thread-pitch entries to your identification draft. Photo estimates require a clear same-plane reference; automatic perspective correction and thread-size recognition are not yet available.

App Layout moved to your avatar menu, under Layout preview. It sets how CrewBarn looks for you in this browser, not for the company, so it no longer sits in the Tool Shed among settings an owner changes for everybody.
The Modules builder now shows where each module appears — which work bar items and which Tool Shed pages it takes with it when you switch it off.
Marketplace Listing, Customer App and Your website now actually disappear when their module is switched off. Those three switches previously changed no menu at all.

Photo teaching now records durable before/after identification and saved lessons, with a paginated trainer-only history. Requires the photo audit database migration and API deployment. Earlier events are not backfilled; other CBI actions are not yet covered.

Teach CBI intake now shows attachments from the matching conversation and refreshes for new photos. Authorized trainers can identify a photo and separately save an explicit reusable lesson. Conversation matching does not automatically associate photos with a job.
Connect settings: Label Printer and Company Files now appear in Connect. Both existed in the Tool Shed but were filed in no Connect section, so they were missing from the settings list entirely.

CBI AI now hides itself when CBI is switched off in your work dashboard, the same way every other module hides its own pages. It used to stay visible and report an active connection while the Ask CBI button was gone from the crew app.

CBI reminder history: open the related invoice in your hosted or self-hosted work dashboard. Draft text is explicitly labeled as a stored excerpt, not a sent message or necessarily the complete draft.

CBI payment reminders now shows recent draft excerpts, failures and skipped runs on the skill page. The API filters activity by task before applying the limit. Draft preparation is clearly distinguished from sending.
Crew right now: action buttons now reserve their full label width. Message and Assign job no longer squeeze their words onto multiple lines.

CBI AI page: if CBI is switched off in your work dashboard, the page now says so and links you straight to the switch. It used to show a green Active connection while the Ask CBI button was missing from every phone — those are two different switches.

Teach CBI: Payment reminders now has its own skill screen with the existing draft toggle, overdue-day schedule and local drafting hour. It keeps human review explicit and does not enable automatic sending.
API Endpoint Guide: added Accounting, Bank feed, Subcontractors and Hiring. That is 63 more endpoints written up with what you can send, what comes back, and which permission each one needs.

Accounting covers the chart of accounts, journal entries, the financial statements and period closes. Bank feed covers matching transactions to invoices and expenses, splitting them, and importing a statement CSV. Nothing else in the guide changed.

CBI knowledge: Edit opens and focuses the rule editor, Forget asks for confirmation and reports failures, and search filters have accessible labels. Removing knowledge does not remove source records or undo past actions.

Teach CBI → What CBI knows: confirmed knowledge is grouped into responsive category cards with amber accents. The teaching form collapses when browsing and opens when editing a rule. Existing filters and controls remain available.

Connect settings: replaced the inner sidebar with horizontal section buttons and a small-screen dropdown across CBI, communications, payments, integrations, appearance, preferences, marketplace and documents. Your main Connect sidebar stays in place; content uses the full row below the section navigation.
Teach CBI → Is this right?: compact review counts, a side queue on wide screens, and side-by-side suggestion/source reading on large displays. Existing approval and correction behavior is unchanged.

Teach CBI overview: a compact teaching entry and real review counts now lead into a responsive responsibility grid. Removed duplicate setup panels and nested card containers; task controls and review links stay available.

CBI AI layout: removed the narrow 1,080px page cap so training uses the available workspace. Navigation is more compact, the connection banner is smaller, and guided setup stays on the provider page instead of crowding every training screen.
Update prompt: Reload now requests a fresh page while keeping your current page and settings tab. Save unfinished edits before reloading.
CBI AI → Teach CBI: review intake, review suggested knowledge, and see each responsibility's current limits from one place.

Train intake: choose hands-on preparation on request or automatic drafts for human review. These modes do not authorize automatic job creation or customer messages. The API and queue workers must be updated to use this control.
Parts corrections: choose a local fix or, with training permission, save a lasting CBI lesson. The correction and lesson save together.
Intake review now shows up to 50 recent events, including local fixes and remembered corrections. This is recent history, not a permanent audit log or readiness score.
Intake retries now protect reviewed drafts, job links, human corrections and review history from late AI results and queue failures.

You can hang a television on the shop wall and put today on it. Settings → Shop TV gives the screen a six-character code, you type that code in once from here, and the TV shows your jobs from then on. No password goes near the television, and nobody standing in your shop can get into CrewBarn from it.

The board is yours to arrange. Drag cards around the TV picture, pull a corner to make one bigger, right-click to add or take one off — and every one of those can also be done with the buttons underneath, so it works on a tablet at the counter. Each card shows your real jobs and crew while you arrange it, not a grey box.

You can build more than one board and have the television take turns through them on a timer you set. A new board starts from a layout rather than an empty grid — Dispatch, Crew wall, Office, Worth chasing (quiet customers, approved estimates, parts you are waiting on), Just a clock, or blank — and each board tab shows a small picture of its own arrangement.

How it looks is picked from pictures rather than lists: dark, light or high contrast shown in their real colours, text size shown at its real size, and the size of your TV drawn to scale from 32″ to 98″ so the letters come out the same height on the wall whichever screen you hung.
You are not asked what resolution the TV is any more. The screen reports it when it checks in, and CrewBarn uses the extra room on a bigger one by itself.
Money is kept off the television by default. Nothing you have not ticked will show a figure to a customer standing in your shop.

Each screen’s card shows a small picture of what is actually on that television, whether it is awake, how big it is and whether money is showing — and “See what it shows” opens the real board in a tab, so you can check a wall without walking over to it.

Fixed: on a day with nothing booked the television showed a built-in layout instead of the board you arranged, and then dropped the cards in it that had nothing to say — so a seven-card board came out as two tiles. Your arrangement now always shows, empty cards included, exactly as the designer draws it.

The designer draws a television now — bezel, stand, and the picture in the background colour you actually picked, so choosing Light no longer shows white cards on a dark wall. Under it sits the size, resolution and grid, and “Preview full screen” opens the real board.

The settings that change how the TV looks — size, screen, background, text — now sit in a column beside the picture, so you can change one and watch the cards change without scrolling. Timing, moments and the money switch stay in the row underneath.
The map on the TV now draws the area you work in even when nobody is out, with a line over it saying so, instead of replacing the whole map with a sentence.
A board with no techs on it now says why — no staff have app access and the field-technician flag yet — instead of “Nobody on the roster”, which read like a fault.

The Dispatch board a new screen starts from now includes what is stuck as well as what is booked: overdue and stalled work, jobs waiting on parts, and customers who have gone quiet. A shop that works from a pile of open jobs rather than booking the day ahead was getting a wall of empty cards.

Fixed: big figures on short cards were cut off on the television — “0 going now” sliced in half at the bottom of a card that looked fine in the designer. The figure is now sized for the card it is in, by the same rule in both places.

The Google Maps setup page now lists the wall board’s addresses. crewbarn.tv is a different top-level domain, so no crewbarn.com wildcard reaches it — miss it and every map works except the one on the TV.

Fixed: on a day with nothing booked the crew card listed everyone as “off today” and pinned them to the bottom of an empty card — while the band above it said “2 techs free”. A tech with nothing booked on an empty day is available, and the card now says so.
List cards show more when they are bigger. Up next, Needs a hand, Gone quiet and Estimates used to show a fixed two or three rows however tall you made the card.

A card holding more than it can show now takes turns through the rest instead of stopping at the third row — Gone quiet, Up next, Needs a hand and Estimates. You set how long each page holds, per screen, under “Long lists”. Set it to Never and a card shows what fits and stops.

Two new cards for the wall, both grouped by person: “Gone quiet, by tech” puts stalled jobs under whoever leads them — worst first, with unassigned work as its own row — and “To do, by tech” shows everybody’s open tasks with a count of who is overdue. A pile says the shop has a problem; a name says whose.

You can now switch company settings on or off per person. Staff → someone → “Company settings” decides whether connect.crewbarn.com opens for them at all; what they can change once inside is still their role and permissions. Nobody loses access on this release — everyone who could sign in still can until you turn someone off.

Fixed: the Portal buttons on Staff went nowhere when you opened Staff from connect.crewbarn.com. The employee portal only exists on the main app, so they now cross to it in a new tab and leave your settings page where it was.

New wall card: “Today, hour by hour” — a lane for each tech, a block for each job at its real time window, and a glowing line showing where now is. Finished jobs fade and strike through so the wall reads as progress; the job in progress glows. The hours shown are the day’s own, so a 9-to-3 day fills the card instead of floating in an empty 6am-to-8pm scale.

The wall can have something behind it: snowfall over a ridge, rain, a fireplace with embers, ocean swell, or drifting light in a rainforest. Pick one under “Behind the board”. Drawn by the television itself, so there is no video to buffer and nothing extra to download.
New card: Weather — the next few hours and any warning worth knowing, from the same forecast the morning huddle reads. Needs your company address set.

You can put your own video or photo behind a wall board — pick “Your own” under Behind the board and upload an MP4, WebM, JPG or PNG up to 40MB. It plays muted and on a loop, because a browser will not start sound by itself and an unattended TV cannot tap its own screen.

Behind the board now offers real footage alongside the painted scenes — pick one under “Or a real one”. These are backdrops CrewBarn provides, so there is nothing to upload and nothing to store in your own space. Your own uploads still work exactly as before.

You can now switch Ask CBI on or off for one person. Settings → Modules still turns it on or off for the whole shop; the new switch on each staff member takes one person out from under that. Nobody loses CBI on this release — it is only off for someone you switch off.

The “Hey CrewBarn” voice settings no longer ask for a Picovoice key. They never needed to — the speech model is built into the crew app and runs on the phone with no signal and nothing sent anywhere. All that is left is the on/off switch.

Automations is now a list of plain sentences instead of a dashboard. Every automatic message CrewBarn sends reads like “1 day before a job, text the customer a reminder”, with a switch beside it. Before, the same rules were spread over five tabs and some of them were labelled things like “invoice.paid → send_email”.

Everything is in one scrolling list, grouped by when it happens: before the job, when a job’s status changes, on the job using GPS, after the job and getting paid, bringing customers back, your own rules, and your other apps. Search it, or narrow it to Customers, Techs, Office or Other apps.
Things you could turn on but have not sit in the same list, marked as suggestions with a Turn on button. One click creates the rule, and a green bar with an Undo appears in case it was the wrong one.

Click any row and the panel on the right shows the actual message — drawn as a text, an email or a phone-app alert — plus where the rule is stored, when it last ran, and who it did not reach and why. Rules you built yourself also get a Send me a test button.

A “Ready to send” row across the top tells you at a glance whether texting, email, templates, reminders and GPS are set up. Anything not ready is amber and links straight to the page that fixes it. This replaces the old setup checklist and template-readiness cards.

Build your own is now one page: a sentence with blanks. “When [you finish a job], wait [1 hour], then [text] [the customer] using [the friendly default].” Tap a blank, pick from the choices, and the next blank opens. The old Customize drawer and the three-step wizard are both gone — this does what they did, in one screen.

Reminders have their own page and are drawn on a job day: customers on the top row, techs on the bottom, from a day before through the start to half an hour after. Each rule is a pin you click to change. Two reminders going out eleven minutes apart is now something you can see rather than something you work out.
The reminder rules moved out of Shop Rules onto that timeline. Shop Rules keeps the master switch and quiet hours, and links across — the same rules, one place to edit them.

The GPS rules that ride on auto check-in — the left-site reminder, the dispatcher alert and the late-arrival warning — now say so plainly instead of showing a switch. They never had one of their own; they run while auto check-in is on. Their numbers are nudged with + and − in the panel.
Two things the backend stores but does not run yet — making a PDF on a status change, and calling another app from one — are marked COMING SOON rather than looking turned on.

The Autopilot card at the top of Automations now counts what actually went out: how many messages CrewBarn sent for you this week, how many are waiting to go, and how many did not send — that last one clicks through to the reason. The count is real; the hours-saved line beside it says "about" because it is two minutes a message, which is a guess.

Text pop-ups show the whole message. They were cut off after two lines, with a third line sliced through the middle so you got the greeting and none of the job — "Good morning Another one for you Noah Stansbury 2022 Jeep grand…" and then nothing useful. The card is taller now and fits seven lines, which is the whole of nearly every text. Anything longer ends with an ellipsis on a clean line instead of half a row of letters.

Payment received pop-ups are live. The card was designed but nothing was behind it — now the moment a payment is recorded, anyone who can see invoices gets it, with the amount, who paid, how, and which job. It fires wherever the money came from: a tech taking a card in a driveway, the customer portal at midnight, a terminal on the counter, or the hourly card-processor sync. Switch it off under toast settings if you would rather not know until morning.

Messages are unread per person now. Before, the first one of you to open a thread marked it read for everybody — so the rest of the office lost the unread mark on a message nobody else had seen. Your Unread list, your Needs action count and the bold rows are yours.

And the thread tells you who has picked it up. Beside each message, in the space next to it, you now see "Read by" and the names of whoever in the office has read that far — you included. Nobody is told they read their own text.

Your Google reviews can come into CrewBarn. Connect your Google Business Profile once under Tool Shed → Google reviews and your reviews are pulled in hourly — you can read them and reply to them without opening another tab, and the reply posts to Google as your business.
Which means the New review pop-up finally works. It only fires for a review that arrived after you connected, so connecting does not set off one pop-up for every review you have ever had.

Fixed: the towns you type into "Where do you work?" now actually get used. They were only being filed as search keywords — the town pages were written from towns you already had customers in, so a brand-new shop asked for three town pages and got none, and the "areas we serve" line on the site listed ZIP codes instead of town names.

You can change the towns you cover after setup. The Service area screen has the same county picker the first-time setup uses, and what you pick is what your site says it covers. Before, that list was fixed the day the site was made.

About and Contact can be edited at last. Every site gets four pages nobody asked for — About, Contact, a services overview and the customer portal page — and the builder could change every page on your site except those. There is an "About & contact" screen now. They are a fixed set, so there is no Add button pretending you could have two About pages.

You can look at your website before anybody else can. "See it first" on the Go live screen opens your real site in a new tab — the same pages a customer gets, not a mock-up — while it is still switched off. The link only works for you and stops working after half an hour. Before this, the first time you saw your own site was the moment it went public.

You can start over. "You already have a website" used to be the end of the road: the setup questions were unreachable once a site existed, so a draft you did not like meant editing every page by hand. There is a Start over option now that asks first and tells you exactly what goes — every word — and what stays: your pictures, colours, logo and web address.

"Write this one for me" is on every service, town and blog page in the builder. The AI wrote your site once at setup and then went quiet — so adding a ninth service afterwards meant writing it yourself, on the screen whose whole point is that you do not have to. Your heading stays; everything under it is replaced.

Label pages remember your label size. Every labels screen opened on "Sheet" and you picked your thermal size again every single time — on every page, every print. It now opens on whatever you printed last, remembered per computer, so the shop PC with the 2x1 printer and the laptop that prints Avery sheets each open on the right one.

Bluetooth label printing stopped asking which printer on every label. It opened the device chooser for each print, so a run of forty asset labels meant picking the same printer forty times. It now reconnects to the one you already allowed, and only asks when there is nothing to reconnect to.

Real Avery sheets are in the label sizes now — 5160, 5161, 5163 and 5167 — and they use Avery’s own measurements, so the labels land on the die-cuts instead of near them. The layout used to work out its own grid and centre it on the page, which is right for blank stock you cut yourself and wrong for every pre-cut sheet made.

Fixed a label size that told you the wrong thing to buy: the 2.25″ × 1.25″ option said “Avery 5160”. Avery 5160 is 2⅝″ × 1″, thirty to a sheet — so anybody who bought 5160 on the strength of that printed a layout that missed every label on it. That option is now marked generic, and real 5160 is its own choice.

Every labels page has a “Coming out the wrong size?” panel with the Windows setup, written for the person standing at the printer holding a bad sheet. It gives different advice for thermal printers and for die-cut sheets, because they fail for different reasons — and it includes the shortcut that removes the print dialog entirely.

Bin labels have a new label studio: a picture of exactly what will come out, next to the questions in plain words — what gets a label, what you are printing on, how many, and what fits on that size. It replaces a toolbar of dropdowns whose real problem was never finding the control, it was not knowing what would come out until it came out. The other label pages follow.

The label studio is on every labels page that prints QR codes: assets, a batch of assets, building placards, bins, purchase order lines and catalog items. Same screen on all of them — a picture of what will come out, beside the questions in plain words.

And what prints now matches what you see. The preview and the printer draw the same face from the same fields: a big QR, the name in heavy type, the code in a typewriter font, a solid black tag for what it is, and a pin for where it lives. The PDF used to draw its own thing, close in spirit and different on paper.

Label printing no longer leaves a PDF tab open behind every print, and it now works with the silent-printing shortcut. Labels used to open in a new tab that printed itself — which meant a shop that set Chrome up to skip the print dialog still got the dialog for every single label, the one thing they set it up to avoid.

New: Tool Shed → Label Printer. Install the small CrewBarn Print Bridge on a shop computer and labels go straight to a printer you pick — no Windows print window, and nothing resizing your 2x1 on the way. It is optional: without it printing works exactly as it does today. A browser cannot choose a printer on its own, which is the only reason this exists.

Once a computer has the Print Bridge connected, the Print button on every labels page sends straight to the printer you picked — no print window, nothing resizing your labels. It says which printer underneath, and there is a link to use the print window instead if you want it for one job. Sticker sheets still go through the print window, because a sheet is a page and only a label can be sent as one.

Fixed the incoming-call pop-up when a caller is a known customer. Three buttons — Call back, Go to customer, Open thread — did not fit across the card: every label broke in half and the last one ran off the edge. They wrap onto a second row now. The pop-up also had a hole in the middle, left over from making the card taller so text messages fit.

The Label Printer page now shows a checksum for the Print Bridge download, with the one-line PowerShell command to check it against. Windows warns about the Print Bridge because it is not signed, and “click Run anyway” is a lot to ask without a way to prove the file is the one CrewBarn built — now there is one.

Label Printer is in the Tool Shed in the app, not in Connect. Pairing a printer is remembered by the browser you pair it in, and a printer is a physical thing on one desk — so it is set up in the place the printing happens. Set up on Connect, the workspace would not have seen it and labels would have quietly kept going through the Windows print window.

If you have arranged your own Tool Shed cards, settings added in later releases now show up on the grid instead of hiding in Customize. Cards you took off stay off — the layout now remembers what it has already offered you, so it can tell "you removed this" apart from "this did not exist yet".

Zebra label printers work now. CrewBarn sends ZPL to a Zebra and ESC/POS to everything else, and works out which from the printer's name — there is a “what it speaks” box on the Label Printer page if the guess is wrong. Before, a Zebra was sent something it does not understand and simply did nothing, which looks exactly like a cable that has fallen out.

Website builder, the towns you cover: each town now says whether it has a page of its own, and one tap makes it — with the town, state and web address already filled in. Before, the list of towns and the pages written for those towns were two separate lists that never spoke, so giving Palm Bay a page meant typing “Palm Bay” into a box directly under a list that already said Palm Bay. A page whose town is not on your list is now pointed out instead of just sitting there.

Reading size now moves all of the text. Under Tool Shed → App Layout, Large and Extra large used to grow the ordinary text and leave the small labels, hints and badges exactly where they were — which made a big monitor look messier rather than easier to read. Nearly two thousand bits of small text were setting their own size and ignoring the setting; they follow it now. If you have not picked a size, nothing changes by a single pixel.

New: a TV board for the shop wall. Open crewbarn.tv on any smart TV, type the code it shows into Tool Shed → Shop TV, and the whole office can see where the crew is, what is booked, what has gone quiet, approved estimates waiting to be scheduled, and what is stuck on parts. Build several boards and set how often it moves between them. Dark, light or high-contrast. Nothing is ever typed on the television, and money stays off the screen unless you turn it on — with it off the figures never leave CrewBarn, so there is nothing there for a customer in your shop to read.

Shop TV boards are arranged by dragging. Tool Shed → Shop TV shows a television-shaped box with the same grid the wall uses: drag a card to move it, drag its corner to resize, or make one fill the whole screen. Cards will not land on top of each other. Build several boards, set how long each stays up, and choose how one gives way to the next — fade, slide, or a straight cut.

Website builder: “What kind of work do you do?” really does start filled in with the trade you picked at signup now. It was announced yesterday and never actually worked — the box was built a split second before your details arrived, so it filled itself in from nothing.

Website builder: “Where do you work?” can fill itself in from your county. Search the county you cover and tap the towns from the list instead of typing them — biggest first, and only the ones you tap are added, because a county holds more towns than anybody works in.

Website builder: a Pictures screen for your main photo, your logo and your site icon — the little icon on the browser tab. All three were only changeable on the old website page before. The preview shows where each one lands, and your logo is used as the site icon until you upload one.

Side menus everywhere got a redesign. Every row in a settings menu, in Connect and in the employee portal now carries a small picture, so you find “Service area” or “Team security” by shape instead of reading eight lines of grey text. The one you have open is a filled tile and a warm card rather than a thin line down the side. The portal’s emoji are gone — they came out differently on every phone.

Fixed: a call from a number CrewBarn does not recognise showed a circle with “(5” in it — the app was reading a phone number as if it were somebody’s name and taking their initials. Unknown callers now get a phone icon. Named customers and staff are unchanged.

The API endpoint guide (Developers → API guide) has been rebuilt to look like the rest of CrewBarn instead of a separate dark-themed product, and two things in it were wrong: it offered an endpoint that was never built, and the sample command you copy had stray characters in it that stopped it running. Both fixed, and a new check now fails if the guide ever describes an endpoint the API does not serve.

Website builder: the main picture, logo and site icon can now be added straight from “Pick how it looks”, instead of only from Pictures two steps later. A photo across the top IS how your site looks, so being sent hunting for it was backwards. Same three uploads either way — add one in one place and it is there in the other.

Fixed: on connect.crewbarn.com, clicking an email or document template did nothing — the list had moved to Connect and the editor behind it had not, so every row opened an address that was not there. Templates open again.
Payments settings now has a side menu — Stripe, GoDaddy, bank transfers and the watched bank account are four screens instead of one long scroll, so you only see the one you came for.

Templates & Forms: the three kinds of template are a side menu now instead of tabs above a long table. Tabs scrolled off the moment you started reading and left you in a list with no sign of which one you were in.

Your Company Cost Model now actually does something. The markup you set is offered when you price a new part, a catalog part that never got a price now goes onto an estimate at cost-plus-markup instead of $0, and an estimate under your minimum service call says so before it goes out. Nothing is ever overwritten — a price you typed stays the price you typed.

Website builder: Pages, Services, Service area and Blog are built — they were the four marked “soon”. Edit the words on your home page, add a page per service and per town you cover, and write posts, all with saving that happens by itself. Pictures per page and raw HTML are still on the older website page.

Fixed: your logo now appears on your website. The Logo tool always said it goes on your website, invoices and quotes — but the site header wrote your company name as text and only used the logo for the browser-tab icon. Shops with no logo still show their name, exactly as before.

Your website can have its own logo now. One logo used to serve invoices, quotes, texts and the website, and the mark that prints well on an invoice is often the wrong shape for a website header. Under Pictures there is a Website logo you can set separately — leave it empty and the site keeps using your main logo.

The website builder now only holds website things. Your business logo — the one on invoices and the customer portal — is set under Brand & Logo, not in here, and the logo maker asks whether a logo you draw is for the website or for everything.

Your website colour and your invoice colour were always separate settings, but the colour screen claimed they were one and showed an invoice and a text message changing colour when neither would. It now says what it does, and offers a button to copy the colour onto your paperwork if you do want them matching.

Fixed, and only shipped this morning: editing your home page’s headline in the new Pages screen saved but changed nothing on the live site — it was writing to a field the website does not read. Headline, the line under it, and the blocks further down now all go where the site looks.
Cloudflare: once your file storage bucket exists, the page says “R2 storage active” and names it, instead of offering to set one up with an unticked box that read as if storage was off.

Go live now shows whether Cloudflare is connected, with a link to connect it if not — it is what using your own web address goes through, and the screen used to say nothing about it. And a domain you have already connected is recognised: if it is waiting on DNS the page says so instead of asking whether you want your own address.

Tester accounts get the whole product now. Being a tester used to mean bring-your-own everything — CrewBarn-managed storage, maps and phone numbers were off the table, so trying a feature meant setting up an account somewhere else first. The beta agreement is unchanged; the floating walkthrough is gone.

Pop-up alerts redesigned. Every one is now the same square with a coloured band that tells you what it is before you read it — a call, a text, a voicemail, an email, an intake. Everything is visible without hovering, the customer is up front, and there is a button for the next step plus Open thread. Hovering the stack pauses every timer so nothing disappears while you are reading it.

Website builder: a new “Why they pick you” screen — your Google rating and review count, how fast you answer, a line a customer actually said, a switch to show your own job photos instead of stock pictures, and the questions people ask on the phone. If you chose the Trust-first home page, this is what fills the strip that was empty.

More of the old website settings are in the builder now: the small line above your headline and the second button (both on the home page screen), a switch for a map of your service area, and the Google verification code that proves the site is yours.

The website builder now asks what you want before it writes. Tell it about your shop in your own words — what to say, what not to mention — choose how many service pages, town pages and blog posts you get, and let it pick a colour that suits your trade. It used to write five service pages and three posts, always, with no idea what you wanted said.
Website builder: “What kind of work do you do?” starts filled in with the trade you picked when you signed up. Change it if you want to say it differently — it just is not a blank box any more.

Connect: “Open CrewBarn” now goes to your own domain if you run CrewBarn on one, whatever plan you are on. It used to only do that on the self-hosted plan, which meant anyone who had not subscribed yet was still sent to app.crewbarn.com.

Setup step “Maps and address lookup” now fills your domain in from the Cloudflare account you already connected, instead of asking you to type it again. Change it if your customers use a different address.

Fixed, and worth knowing if you set up a Google Maps key from Connect recently: the website addresses to copy into Google were taken from whichever CrewBarn page you were on. From connect.crewbarn.com that produced the settings console — which is not where maps run. Restricting your key to that list would have switched maps off in the app. It now lists app.crewbarn.com, and your own domain if you self-host.

Fixed a dead end in AI setup: you picked Claude, pressed “Set up the key”, and the key screen sent you back to pick an AI — because the pick was still sitting unsaved behind a Save button. Picking now saves straight away, says so, and takes you on to the key. There is an Undo if you picked the wrong one, and the key setup has a Cancel on every step instead of only the first.

The staff list is easier to read. It was an eight-column table with about a dozen things crammed into every row; it is a list of people now — initials, name, role, then their contact line, then the field rules. Everything that was there is still there and still one click. Two changes you will notice: the rules say ✓ or ○ instead of being struck through in tiny grey, and rows no longer all shout “ACTIVE” — only the ones that need you do, so “Invite sent” and “No longer here” actually stand out.

Staff → Pay is rebuilt. It used to show all eighteen boxes whatever you picked, so somebody on a flat hourly rate was asked for a commission percentage, a commission basis and a parts cap. Now you pick how they are paid first and only the rest that applies shows. “A cut of what” says what each option means — what the job sold for, what was left after parts, or what the customer actually paid — because that last difference decides who carries an unpaid invoice. And the worked example starts filled in from their own normal week, so it shows what a week costs you straight away instead of after you fill five boxes.

Setup step “Where your photos and maps come from”: instead of making a bucket and an API token yourself and copying four values across, you paste one Cloudflare token and CrewBarn makes the bucket and fills the keys in. The same token is what gives your website its own web address and lets you run CrewBarn on your own domain later — one connection, three jobs. Typing the values in by hand is still there, folded away, for a bucket you already have.

Payments is being split up. “Let customers pay by bank transfer” and “Watch your bank for payments” are now their own pages, each saying what actually happens — including that “I've sent it” is a promise, not a payment, and the invoice stays unpaid until the money lands. And the question everyone asks about the bank connection is answered before it is asked: Stripe does the connecting and nothing else, no Stripe account, no money through them, read-only.

New page: “Where your email comes from” — the one part of the phone/text/email screen every shop needs. It now says what it is for (keeping your quotes out of the junk folder) and what happens if you skip it, instead of telling you what “most tenants” should do.

The AI settings page is now seven focused pages instead of one screen with six tabs: which AI does the thinking, your key, what it is allowed to do, what it picks up as you work, what it has learned, talking to CBI, and what it has been doing. The old page still opens if you have it bookmarked.

“What AI has learned” is a queue with two answers. Anything waiting on you comes first with “That is right” and “No, drop it”, and you can see the call or note it read before deciding. What it is already using is listed underneath, so “what does it think it knows about my shop” has an answer you can read — and delete.
“What AI has been doing” puts the money first: what the last twenty jobs cost on your own AI account, and how many did not work. Each line says what it was in plain words rather than a task code.

Setup step “Get your crew in”: roles are cards that say what each person will be able to see, not a dropdown.
